system_prompt:
You are a strategy analyst investigating an opportunity for a manufacturer. Use these tools:
read_brief {} : read the company, the question and your budgets.
frame_problem {"objective":"...","constraints":["..."],"alternatives":["..."]} : state the real objective and the options, including ones the question did not suggest. Accepted once.
search_evidence {"query":"..."} : keyword search of the evidence. Uses one search.
challenge_theory {"theory_id":"T1","query":"..."} : search for evidence that could prove a theory wrong. Uses one search.
read_source {"id":"..."} : read a result found by search.
add_theory {"claim":"...","who_benefits":"...","why_behaviour_changes":"...","how_value_is_captured":"...","assumptions":["..."],"predictions":["..."]} : add one causal theory of value. Returns its id.
assess_evidence {"theory_id":"T1","evidence_id":"...","direction":"supports or contradicts or neutral","quote":"exact words from the source","evidence_kind":"company_assertion or customer_observation or independent_study or regulation or analogy or market_fact","does_not_show":"what this evidence cannot establish"} : say how evidence bears on a theory, honestly. Use neutral if it does neither.
propose_test {"name":"...","theories":["T1","T2"],"method":"...","sample":"...","measure":"...","prediction_by_theory":{"T1":"...","T2":"..."},"decision_rule":"...","cost_eur":N,"weeks":N} : design an experiment where the theories predict different results.
revise_theory {"theory_id":"T1","status":"kept or revised or rejected","reason":"...","new_claim":"the changed claim, or none","evidence_ids":["..."]} : update a theory after new evidence.
finish {"recommendation":"...","target_customer":"...","value_proposition":"...","favoured_theory":"T1","next_action":"...","uncertainty":"...","would_change_if":["..."],"evidence_ids":["..."]} : end the investigation.

Reply with one JSON object: {"name": "<tool>", "arguments": {...}}. A user turn that starts with "Tool result:" is the output of your call. End by calling finish.

Work like a scientist, not a consultant.
1. read_brief, then frame_problem. List at least three alternatives, including no expansion and options the question did not suggest.
2. Search before you theorise. Find out what the company already sells to individual buyers, and do not assume. Read at least three sources.
3. add_theory at least twice, and a third time if you have a different cause. A theory is a causal explanation of why people behave as they do, not advice. Do not write "the company should". Each theory needs a different cause: who benefits, why they would change behaviour, how the manufacturer captures value. Give assumptions, and predictions someone could measure.
For example, from eyewear: "People treat glasses as a medical necessity. If they came to see them as fashion, they would own several pairs, so a maker that controls design and retail could earn premium prices." A rival theory would name a different cause.
4. assess_evidence for every theory, quoting the source's exact words. Say what kind of evidence it is and what it cannot show. A company's own claim is not proof of demand. Use challenge_theory to look for evidence that could prove your favoured theory wrong. If you find nothing against it, say so. Never force a contradiction.
5. propose_test: an affordable experiment where the theories predict different results, with a decision rule that has a threshold.
6. If new evidence arrives, read it and use revise_theory.
7. finish. Say what you recommend, the next action, what is uncertain, and what would change your mind.

Every number or fact you present as observed must come from a source you read. Numbers you propose, such as a test's sample, budget, duration, threshold or an estimate, are allowed when you label them as proposed or estimated. Your theories are hypotheses, not facts. Results marked SIMULATED are not real demand, so never cite one in finish.

A controller opens the tools for each stage, and each tool result lists them. Before you finish you will also use:
decline_test {"reason":"..."} : say why more information is not worth its cost here, instead of proposing a test.
state_position {"favoured_theory":"T1","recommendation":"...","beliefs":{"T1":"likely","T2":"uncertain"}} : say what you believe now, rating each theory very unlikely, unlikely, uncertain, likely or very likely. finish then also takes "beliefs".
A SIMULATED result is a what-if exercise. Reason as if it were real, and say what it would mean for your theories. A result can change nothing. Still keep it out of the evidence you cite.

Each turn shows the current state of the investigation, including what you already tried. Do not repeat a call listed there.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Drägerwerk AG & Co. KGaA investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B medical and safety technology.
constraints: Limited to publicly available information; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Must assess demand, competitive landscape, regulatory feasibility, and value capture mechanisms.
Must consider existing consumer reach (if any) and potential regulatory hurdles for consumer products.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home gas detection, personal protective equipment, or alcohol/drug testing for individuals).
2) Expand the existing B2B portfolio into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., licensing safety technology to consumer brands).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current B2B markets (hospitals, industry, fire services, police).
4) Partner with established consumer brands to co‑develop and distribute a consumer product, leveraging existing distribution channels.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated home gas detector if it is marketed as a safety necessity and backed by clear regulatory compliance, because they currently lack awareness and trust in CO alarms.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners and renters who face CO risks from cooking, heating, or ventilation.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Increased awareness of CO poisoning risks and a trusted recommendation from a medical/safety brand will motivate purchase beyond price sensitivity.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Dräger can charge a premium for a compliant, certified device and capture recurring revenue through accessories and service, leveraging its safety brand credibility.
assumptions: Regulatory environment allows consumer CO detector certification.
Consumers trust safety brand recommendations over price alone.
Marketing can effectively communicate safety benefits to a non-technical audience.
predictions: In a test offering a compliant CO detector at a price comparable to non-compliant models, purchase intent will be at least 15% higher than for a non-compliant alternative.
Surveyed buyers will cite safety concern as the primary reason for purchase.
T1.first_claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated home gas detector if it is marketed as a safety necessity and backed by clear regulatory compliance, because they currently lack awareness and trust in CO alarms.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated home gas detector if it is positioned as a lifestyle accessory or fashion item, because they view safety devices as status symbols rather than purely functional items.
T2.who_benefits: Style-conscious consumers who value design and brand identity.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Exposure to design-focused marketing and social proof (e.g., influencer endorsements) shifts perception from utilitarian to aspirational, increasing willingness to pay a premium.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Dräger can command higher prices for design-led products and capture recurring revenue through accessories, limited editions, and brand extensions, leveraging its safety reputation as a design asset.
assumptions: Consumers associate safety brands with premium aesthetics.
Social media and influencer marketing can effectively influence purchase decisions for non-functional products.
Regulatory compliance can be satisfied without compromising design.
predictions: In a test offering a design-focused CO detector at a premium price, purchase intent will be at least 20% higher than for a functional, low‑priced alternative.
Buyers will cite design and brand appeal as the primary reason for purchase.
T2.first_claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated home gas detector if it is positioned as a lifestyle accessory or fashion item, because they view safety devices as status symbols rather than purely functional items.

position.recommendation: Invest in a safety-focused consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home CO detector) before broader consumer expansion. The evidence shows existing consumer demand for CO alarms and a regulatory environment that allows consumer certification, supporting T1.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Drägerwerk AG & Co. KGaA investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B medical and safety technology.
constraints: Limited to publicly available information; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Must assess demand, competitive landscape, regulatory feasibility, and value capture mechanisms.
Must consider existing consumer reach (if any) and potential regulatory hurdles for consumer products.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home gas detection, personal protective equipment, or alcohol/drug testing for individuals).
2) Expand the existing B2B portfolio into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., licensing safety technology to consumer brands).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current B2B markets (hospitals, industry, fire services, police).
4) Partner with established consumer brands to co‑develop and distribute a consumer product, leveraging existing distribution channels.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated home gas detector if it is marketed as a safety necessity and backed by clear regulatory compliance, because they currently lack awareness and trust in CO alarms.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners and renters who face CO risks from cooking, heating, or ventilation.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Increased awareness of CO poisoning risks and a trusted recommendation from a medical/safety brand will motivate purchase beyond price sensitivity.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Dräger can charge a premium for a compliant, certified device and capture recurring revenue through accessories and service, leveraging its safety brand credibility.
assumptions: Regulatory environment allows consumer CO detector certification.
Consumers trust safety brand recommendations over price alone.
Marketing can effectively communicate safety benefits to a non-technical audience.
predictions: In a test offering a compliant CO detector at a price comparable to non-compliant models, purchase intent will be at least 15% higher than for a non-compliant alternative.

Track click-through rate (CTR) and conversion rate (purchase intent) for each variant.
X1.sample: Estimated 5,000 adult visitors to a consumer safety website, split equally between the two ad variants.
X1.measure: CTR and conversion rate (purchase intent) for each variant.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Safety variant will achieve a CTR of at least 2% and a conversion rate of at least 1.5% among homeowners; lifestyle variant will achieve a CTR of at least 1.5% and a conversion rate of at least 1%.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Lifestyle variant will achieve a CTR of at least 2% and a conversion rate of at least 1.5% among homeowners; safety variant will achieve a CTR of at least 1.5% and a conversion rate of at least 1%.

If the lifestyle variant meets both its thresholds, develop a lifestyle-focused proposition. final.recommendation: Invest in a safety-focused consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home CO detector) before broader consumer expansion. The evidence shows existing consumer demand for CO alarms and a regulatory environment that allows consumer certification, supporting T1.
final.target_customer: Homeowners and renters who face CO risks from cooking, heating, or ventilation.
final.value_proposition: A compliant, reliable home gas detector marketed as a safety necessity, backed by Dräger’s safety brand credibility, offering peace of mind and potential recurring revenue through accessories and service.
final.next_action: Run the proposed digital messaging test (5,000 visitors, two ad variants) to validate purchase intent for a safety-focused proposition. If thresholds are met, proceed to develop the product; otherwise, focus on B2B markets.
final.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market and willingness to pay a premium for a differentiated product are uncertain. Regulatory feasibility for consumer certification and competitive response from established consumer brands are also unknown.
would_change_if: If the test shows the lifestyle variant achieving its thresholds, we would shift to a lifestyle-focused proposition.

X1.name: Home Gas Detector Purchase Intent Test
X1.method: Online controlled experiment with two between‑subjects conditions. Participants view a product description of a compliant home CO detector (T1) or a design‑focused home gas detector (T2). Both versions are priced at a premium comparable to non‑compliant alternatives. Participants indicate purchase intent on a 7‑point scale (1‑not likely to 7‑very likely) and state the primary reason for purchase.
X1.sample: 400 adults (200 per condition) recruited via an online panel to match demographic distribution of target consumers (homeowners, renters, age 25‑55).
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑90) and primary reason for purchase (open‑ended).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and primary reason of safety concern for the compliant version than for the design version.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and primary reason of design/brand appeal for the design version than for the compliant version.

X1.decision_rule: If the design version’s purchase intent is at least 15 percentage points higher than the compliant version and at least 20 percentage points above the baseline (1), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If the compliant version’s purchase intent is at least 15 percentage points higher and the design version is not significantly better, focus on safety‑driven B2B expansion. If neither condition meets the thresholds, do not invest.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home CO detector) that emphasizes safety compliance and awareness, rather than a lifestyle or fashion proposition. Begin with a low‑cost test of purchase intent for a compliant CO detector to validate demand before scaling.
final.target_customer: Homeowners and renters who face CO risks from cooking, heating, or ventilation.
final.value_proposition: A trusted, compliant home gas detector that raises awareness of CO poisoning risks and provides peace of mind, leveraging Dräger’s safety brand credibility to justify a premium price.
final.next_action: Run the proposed 10‑week, €18,000 online purchase‑intent test with 400 adults, comparing a compliant CO detector to a design‑focused alternative. Use the decision rule to decide whether to proceed with development.
final.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market for home gas detectors and the willingness to pay a premium for compliance are uncertain. Regulatory feasibility for consumer products is also unknown.
would_change_if: If the test shows the design version’s purchase intent is at least 15 percentage points higher than the compliant version and at least 20 percentage points above the baseline, we would shift focus to a lifestyle proposition.
If the test fails to meet the thresholds or shows no significant difference, we would recommend no expansion and continue focusing on B2B markets.

arguments.sample: Proposed sample: 500 adults in Germany (n=250 per frame) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and home ownership. Recruitment budget €2,000 for panel access.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent rate (percentage of participants indicating "Would buy") and the proportion of buyers citing the stated reason (safety vs. design).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Purchase intent for the safety‑focused frame will be at least 15 percentage points higher than for the lifestyle frame.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Purchase intent for the lifestyle‑focused frame will be at least 15 percentage points higher than for the safety‑focused frame.

arguments.decision_rule: If the safety‑frame intent ≥ 15% and the lifestyle‑frame intent ≤ 15%, conclude T1 is supported and T2 is not. If the lifestyle‑frame intent ≥ 15% and the safety‑frame intent ≤ 15%, conclude T2 is supported and T1 is not. If neither threshold is met, the evidence is inconclusive and further testing is needed.

Participants view two product concepts for a home gas detector: (A) Safety‑focused version marketed as a medical‑grade, regulatory‑compliant device for CO and gas detection; (B) Lifestyle‑focused version marketed as a design‑led, premium‑priced accessory with aesthetic features. Each concept includes a price point and a brief description. Participants indicate whether they would purchase each concept and state the primary reason for their choice.
X1.sample: 500 adults in Germany (n = 250 per condition) recruited via an online panel to ensure demographic diversity.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: would purchase) and primary reason for choice (open‑ended). Secondary measure: willingness to pay (WTP) in euros.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Safety‑focused concept will achieve at least 15% higher purchase intent than lifestyle‑focused concept, and safety concern will be the primary reason for purchase.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Lifestyle‑focused concept will achieve at least 20% higher purchase intent than safety‑focused concept, and design/brand appeal will be the primary reason for purchase.

X1.decision_rule: If the purchase intent difference between the two concepts is at least 10 percentage points, proceed to develop the higher‑intent proposition. If the difference is less than 10 percentage points, consider both concepts but prioritize safety‑focused positioning due to evidence of consumer demand for safety‑branded devices.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer reducing packing errors and does not address consumer demand for home gas detectors, safety positioning, or lifestyle appeal. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home CO detector) that emphasizes safety compliance, regulatory certification, and trust in a medical/safety brand. Begin with a small-scale pilot test to validate purchase intent and primary purchase reason before scaling.
final.target_customer: Homeowners and renters in Germany who face CO risks from cooking, heating, or ventilation.
final.value_proposition: A compliant, certified home gas detector that provides reliable safety monitoring, backed by Dräger’s safety brand credibility, offering peace of mind and potential recurring revenue through accessories and service.
final.next_action: Run the proposed 8‑week, €18,000 online choice‑based conjoint survey with 500 German adults to measure purchase intent and primary reason for each concept.
final.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market for home gas detectors and the willingness to pay a premium for safety‑branded products are uncertain. Regulatory feasibility for consumer CO detectors is also unknown.
would_change_if: If the pilot shows purchase intent below 10% or if the primary reason for purchase is not safety concern, we would reconsider the safety‑focused approach and explore lifestyle positioning.
If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for design‑led safety products, we would revise the strategy to prioritize lifestyle positioning.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home gas detection, personal protective equipment, or alcohol/drug testing for individuals).

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Drägerwerk AG & Co. KGaA investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B medical and safety technology.
constraints: Limited to publicly available information; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Must assess demand, competitive landscape, regulatory feasibility, and value capture mechanisms.
Must consider existing consumer reach (if any) and potential regulatory hurdles for consumer products.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home gas detection, personal protective equipment, or alcohol/drug testing for individuals).
2) Expand the existing B2B portfolio into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., licensing safety technology to consumer brands).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current B2B markets (hospitals, industry, fire services, police).
4) Partner with established consumer brands to co‑develop and distribute a consumer product, leveraging existing distribution channels.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: Increased awareness of CO poisoning risks and a trusted recommendation from a medical/safety brand will motivate purchase beyond price sensitivity.

predictions: In a test offering a compliant CO detector at a price comparable to non-compliant models, purchase intent will be at least 15% higher than for a non-compliant alternative.

X1.name: Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Home Gas Detector
X1.method: Online survey with randomized message exposure. Participants view a product description of a compliant home gas detector (T1) or a design-focused lifestyle version (T2). They are asked to state their maximum price they would pay and the reason for choosing the product.
X1.sample: 500 adults (age 18-65) recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and geographic region to reflect general German consumer base.
X1.measure: Maximum price willing to pay (EUR) and primary reason for purchase (safety vs. design/brand appeal).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Mean price willingness to pay for the compliant detector will be at least 15% higher than for the design-focused version.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Mean price willingness to pay for the design-focused version will be at least 20% higher than for the compliant version.

X1.decision_rule: If the design-focused version's mean price is at least 20% higher than the compliant version's mean price, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition focused on lifestyle. If the compliant version's mean price is at least 15% higher, justify investment in a safety‑focused consumer product. If neither threshold is met, do not expand into consumer markets.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer reducing packing errors and does not address consumer demand for home gas detectors, safety awareness, or Dräger's value capture. Therefore it provides no support or contradiction to T1.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home gas detection) that emphasizes regulatory compliance and safety necessity, rather than a lifestyle or fashion proposition. Begin with a small-scale willingness-to-pay survey to validate price sensitivity and demand before scaling.
final.target_customer: Homeowners and renters in Germany who face CO risks from cooking, heating, or ventilation.
final.value_proposition: A compliant, certified home gas detector marketed as a safety necessity, backed by Dräger’s medical safety brand credibility, offering peace of mind and potential recurring revenue through accessories and service.
final.next_action: Run the proposed willingness-to-pay survey (500 adults, 10 weeks, €18,000) to test price sensitivity and demand for a compliant versus design-focused version.
final.uncertainty: Demand for a differentiated consumer product is uncertain; the survey will resolve whether price sensitivity and safety awareness justify investment. Regulatory feasibility and competitive landscape also remain unknown.
would_change_if: If the survey shows the design-focused version's mean price is at least 20% higher than the compliant version, indicating lifestyle demand, the recommendation would shift to a lifestyle proposition.
If the survey fails to meet the price thresholds or shows low purchase intent, the investment would be reconsidered or the consumer expansion would be delayed.

X1.name: Consumer Messaging Test: Energy Efficiency vs. Status Position
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of homeowners (n=500) who have shown interest in home energy efficiency. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two message conditions: (A) Energy efficiency messaging emphasizing accuracy, affordability, and accessibility through retail partners; (B) Status messaging emphasizing professional-grade precision, design, and brand prestige. After viewing the assigned message, participants indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay for a Testo energy measurement kit.
X1.sample: 500 homeowners recruited from an online panel, balanced for age, income, and prior home energy concern.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price willingness to pay for a Testo kit.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in the energy efficiency condition compared to the status condition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in the status condition compared to the energy efficiency condition.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent in the energy efficiency condition is at least 10 points higher than in the status condition, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on energy efficiency. If the difference is less than 5 points, consider a broader consumer proposition or partner approach. If the status condition outperforms, pursue a premium lifestyle positioning.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition focused on home energy efficiency, leveraging Testo's existing retail presence (e.g., Target) and positioning accuracy, affordability, and accessibility. Begin with a limited pilot to test purchase intent and willingness to pay before scaling.
final.target_customer: Homeowners and small businesses in the United States who are concerned about energy costs and seek reliable measurement tools for home efficiency.
final.value_proposition: A Testo energy measurement kit that combines professional-grade accuracy with clear, actionable insights to help consumers reduce energy bills and improve home comfort, sold through familiar retail channels.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Messaging Test (500 homeowners, 8 weeks, €15,000) to compare energy efficiency vs. status messaging. Use the decision rule: if energy efficiency messaging yields at least a 10-point higher purchase intent, proceed;
final.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market and willingness to pay a premium for Testo products are uncertain. Evidence shows strong consumer reach (1.5M+ devices sold) but no proof of premium pricing or status-driven demand.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent for the status condition exceeding energy efficiency by at least 10 points, we would shift focus to a premium lifestyle positioning.
If market research reveals low price sensitivity or low overall consumer demand, we would reconsider expansion or partner approach.

X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging and purchase offer

final.uncertainty: The actual demand for a differentiated consumer proposition is uncertain; the test will determine whether homeowners are willing to pay a premium for a professional-grade energy efficiency tool.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent below 5% or the convenience-focused group wins by a significant margin, the investment would be reconsidered in favor of maintaining the B2B focus or exploring other alternatives.

Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment
Need to verify current consumer reach and demand for Testo instruments
Investment must be justified by evidence of consumer willingness to pay and market opportunity
alternatives: Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home DIY, small businesses, or general consumers)
Expand the existing product portfolio to include additional use cases without a differentiated consumer proposition
Maintain current B2B focus and not pursue consumer expansion

T1.claim: Homeowners will adopt Testo portable measuring instruments if they experience a sudden, high-cost home energy issue (e.g., a sudden rise in heating bills, a confirmed leak, or a mold problem) and need a quick, affordable way to diagnose the problem.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners who face unexpected, costly home energy issues and lack the expertise or tools to diagnose them.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: The sudden, high-cost issue creates an urgent need for a solution; Testo instruments provide a quick, affordable way to identify the cause, reducing the homeowner's anxiety and cost.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Testo sells instruments directly to consumers at a premium price, capturing value through higher margins on a single product sold to a new segment.
assumptions: Homeowners are willing to pay for a tool that can resolve a sudden, high-cost energy issue.
The issue is frequent enough to create a recurring demand for a diagnostic tool.
Testo can reach consumers through retail partners or direct online sales.
predictions: A survey of homeowners with recent high-cost energy bills will show a higher intent to purchase Testo instruments than a survey of homeowners without such bills.
Sales of Testo instruments in regions with high energy bill increases will be higher than in regions with stable bills.

T2.claim: Homeowners will adopt Testo portable measuring instruments if they are aware of and trust the brand through trusted sources such as retailers, community programs, or online reviews, rather than because of a sudden, high-cost home energy issue.
T2.who_benefits: Homeowners who already trust Testo for professional use and are looking for a reliable tool for home-related tasks.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Trust in the brand reduces purchase hesitation and makes the product more attractive than a tool sold on a sudden, high-cost issue.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Testo sells instruments through retail partners and online channels, capturing value through higher margins on a product already trusted by consumers.
assumptions: Homeowners are aware of Testo through trusted channels.
Brand trust translates into purchase intent.
Retail and online channels can effectively reach homeowners.
predictions: A survey of homeowners who have purchased Testo instruments will show higher trust ratings compared to homeowners who have not purchased Testo.

X1.name: Brand Trust vs Sudden Energy Issue Purchase Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios and brand trust measurement.
X1.sample: 500 homeowners recruited from Europe and North America, split equally between two groups: Group A (sudden energy issue) and Group B (brand trust).
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and brand trust rating (1-5).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent than Group B, even when presented with a sudden energy issue scenario.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent than Group A, even when presented with a sudden energy issue scenario.

X1.decision_rule: If purchase intent in Group A is at least 10 percentage points higher than in Group B, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting sudden energy issues. If purchase intent in Group B is at least 10 percentage points higher than in Group A, focus on building brand trust. If neither difference is significant, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.

final.value_proposition: A Testo portable measuring instrument specifically marketed for sudden energy issues, sold through retail partners and online channels, capturing premium margins on a new consumer segment.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Brand Trust vs Sudden Energy Issue Purchase Test (500 homeowners, 8 weeks, €15,000) to validate purchase intent differences between sudden issue and brand trust groups.
final.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market and the exact willingness to pay for a differentiated product are uncertain; the test will clarify whether homeowners act on sudden energy issues or brand trust.

X1.name: Consumer Messaging Test: Premium vs Regulatory Messaging
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of homeowners and renters in regions with varying water quality regulations. Participants view a product page for a home water testing kit and are randomly assigned to one of two messaging conditions: (A) premium positioning emphasizing independent monitoring and peace of mind; (B) regulatory positioning emphasizing compliance with local water quality laws and mandatory testing.
X1.sample: 400 participants (200 per condition) from the US, recruited via an online panel, stratified by region and homeownership status.
X1.measure: Primary outcome: purchase intent measured as the proportion of participants who indicate they would purchase the kit at the stated price. Secondary outcomes: willingness to pay (WTP) for the kit and intent to purchase a subscription service for follow-up testing.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Condition A will generate higher purchase intent and WTP than Condition B, because the premium message resonates with consumers seeking control and peace of mind.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Condition B will generate higher purchase intent and WTP than Condition A, because regulatory messaging motivates compliance-driven purchases.

X1.decision_rule: If purchase intent in Condition A exceeds Condition B by at least 10 percentage points, proceed to develop a premium consumer proposition. If Condition B exceeds Condition A by at least 10 percentage points, pursue a regulatory positioning. If the difference is below 10 points, conduct further testing to resolve ambiguity.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners and renters who seek independent water quality monitoring, positioning the product as a premium peace-of-mind solution. Begin with a limited launch of a premium test kit and accessories, leveraging existing distribution channels to test consumer demand before scaling.
final.target_customer: Homeowners and renters in regions with moderate to high water quality concerns who currently rely on utility or professional testing.
final.value_proposition: Provide accurate, independent water quality testing at home, offering peace of mind and control over drinking water quality, with recurring revenue from test strips and optional follow-up services.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Messaging Test (400 participants, 8 weeks, €15,000) to compare premium vs. regulatory messaging. Use the decision rule: if premium messaging yields a ≥10-point higher purchase intent, proceed to develop the premium
final.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market and actual purchase intent are unknown. Regulatory demand is uncertain; evidence shows kits are widely available but does not confirm consumer adoption or willingness to pay.
would_change_if: If the Consumer Messaging Test shows regulatory messaging generates ≥10 points higher purchase intent, shift focus to compliance positioning.
If sales data from existing B2B channels reveal strong demand for water-quality instruments, reconsider the consumer proposition.
If new evidence shows strong regulatory enforcement in target regions, reinforce the T2 hypothesis and prioritize compliance messaging.

T1.how_value_is_captured: Hach can capture value through recurring sales of test strips, accessories, and potentially bundled subscription services for data analysis or follow-up testing.

X1.name: Messaging Test: Voluntary vs Regulatory Home Water Test Kit
X1.method: Online survey experiment with two randomized messaging conditions. Participants are screened by region (e.g., states with strict water quality laws vs states without). Each participant sees one of two product descriptions of a Hach home water test kit.
X1.sample: 500 participants: 250 from a state with strict water quality laws and 250 from a state without. Recruited via an online panel to match demographic distribution.
X1.measure: Purchase intent measured as a binary choice: "Would you purchase this test kit?" and willingness to pay (WTP) in euros.

prediction_by_theory.T1: In the voluntary messaging condition, purchase intent will be at least 15 percentage points higher than in the regulatory messaging condition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: In the regulatory messaging condition, purchase intent will be at least 15 percentage points higher than in the voluntary messaging condition.

X1.decision_rule: If voluntary purchase intent exceeds regulatory purchase intent by at least 15 percentage points in both regions, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting voluntary consumers. If regulatory purchase intent exceeds voluntary purchase intent by at least 15 percentage points in both regions, pursue a compliance-focused proposition. If neither condition is met, do not expand into consumer markets.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Public evidence shows home water test kits are widely available and sold under Hach brands, but it does not demonstrate consumer demand, willingness to pay, or that consumers will act on the results. A limited messaging test (e.g., voluntary vs regulatory positioning) is needed to validate demand before committing resources.
final.target_customer: Individual homeowners and renters who are concerned about water quality but currently rely on utility or professional testing.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition that positions Hach's home water test kits as a voluntary, peace-of-mind monitoring solution, leveraging existing brand trust and distribution channels.
final.next_action: Run the proposed messaging test (voluntary vs regulatory positioning) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay across regions with different water quality regulations.
final.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market, actual purchase intent, and the price sensitivity of consumers are uncertain. Public evidence does not confirm demand or that consumers will act on the results.
would_change_if: If the messaging test shows voluntary purchase intent exceeding regulatory purchase intent by at least 15 percentage points in both regions, we would proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting voluntary consumers.
If the test shows regulatory purchase intent exceeding voluntary purchase intent by at least 15 percentage points in both regions, we would pursue a compliance-focused proposition.
If neither condition is met, we would maintain the current B2B focus and not expand into consumer markets.

X1.name: Consumer Intent Test: Willingness to Pay for Home Water Test Kit
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging and a willingness-to-pay (WTP) question. Participants are recruited from a panel matching the demographic distribution of homeowners in regions with varying water quality regulations. Participants are shown a product description of a home water test kit and asked: "How much would you pay for a single test kit?" They also indicate whether they would purchase it if it were required by a local regulation (T2) or if they already own a test kit (T1).
X1.sample: 500 participants (150 from regions with strict water quality laws and 150 from regions with moderate laws), balanced for age, gender, and income.
X1.measure: Average WTP for a single test kit (EUR) and binary purchase intent (required by regulation vs. already own kit).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher average WTP and purchase intent in regions with strict water quality laws compared to moderate laws.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher average WTP and purchase intent in regions with strict water quality laws compared to moderate laws.

X1.decision_rule: If the average WTP for a single test kit in the strict-law group exceeds the average WTP in the moderate-law group by at least €10, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting that segment. If the difference is less than €10, the evidence is insufficient to justify investment and no further action is recommended.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners concerned about water quality, leveraging the existing AquaChek brand and distribution channels. Begin with a limited launch of a premium test kit marketed as a peace-of-mind solution, and gather real purchase data before scaling.
final.target_customer: Individual homeowners and renters in regions with moderate to strict water quality regulations who currently rely on utility or professional testing.
final.value_proposition: A premium home water test kit that provides independent, accurate water quality monitoring, offering peace of mind and the ability to act on results, while maintaining Hach’s reputation for reliability.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Intent Test (or a smaller pilot) to validate willingness to pay and purchase intent. Use the results to decide whether to scale the product or pivot to a different use case.
final.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market and actual purchase behavior are uncertain; evidence shows kits are widely available but does not confirm consumer demand or price sensitivity.
would_change_if: If the Consumer Intent Test shows average willingness to pay for a single test kit is below €20, indicating price sensitivity, the recommendation would shift toward a lower‑cost entry point or a different value proposition.
If new evidence shows strong regulatory demand in specific regions, the recommendation would shift toward a compliance‑focused product line rather than a peace‑of‑mind proposition.

X1.name: Consumer Intent Test: Willingness to Pay vs Regulatory Compliance
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.
X1.sample: 500 respondents: 250 in a region with strict water quality laws (e.g., California) and 250 in a region without such laws (e.g., Texas). Recruit via panel to match demographics.
X1.measure: 1) WTP for a premium home water test kit (e.g., $25 for 50 test strips). 2) Intent to purchase a kit marketed as required by regulation versus a voluntary health-monitoring kit.

prediction_by_theory.T1: WTP for the voluntary health-monitoring kit will be higher than for the compliance kit in both regions.
prediction_by_theory.T2: WTP for the compliance kit will be higher than for the voluntary kit in the region with strict laws, and both regions will show similar WTP for the voluntary kit.

X1.decision_rule: If the average WTP for the voluntary kit in the region with strict laws exceeds the WTP for the compliance kit by at least $5, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for voluntary health monitoring. If the average WTP for the compliance kit in the region without strict laws exceeds the WTP for the voluntary kit by at least $5, prioritize a compliance-focused proposition. If both regions show similar WTP for the voluntary kit, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a warehouse label printer and packing errors, which does not address consumer demand, willingness to pay, or regulatory compliance for home water testing kits. Therefore it provides no support or contradiction to T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public evidence shows home water test kits are widely available (market fact) but does not demonstrate consumer demand, willingness to pay, or intent to purchase. Conduct the proposed Consumer Intent Test to validate whether voluntary health-monitoring demand outweighs compliance demand before committing resources.
final.target_customer: Individual homeowners and renters who are concerned about water quality but currently rely on utility or professional testing.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition that positions Hach's home water testing kits as a voluntary, health-monitoring tool for independent water quality assessment, leveraging existing distribution channels to reach consumers.
final.next_action: Run the Consumer Intent Test (500 respondents, 6 weeks, €18,000) to measure willingness to pay for a premium test kit and intent to purchase a voluntary health-monitoring kit versus a compliance-focused kit.
final.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market, actual purchase intent, and the relative strength of voluntary health-monitoring demand versus regulatory compliance demand are uncertain.
would_change_if: If the Consumer Intent Test shows that compliance demand (required by regulation) generates significantly higher willingness to pay than voluntary health-monitoring demand, we would prioritize a compliance-focused proposition.
If the test reveals that consumers are unwilling to pay a premium for a home water test kit, we would reconsider the consumer expansion strategy.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Hach Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B water-quality analysis instruments.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment

Must consider existing B2B customer base and current product portfolio
Any recommendation must be based on observable demand, not assumptions
alternatives: Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home water testing, pool water testing, or personal health monitoring)

Maintain current B2B focus and not pursue consumer expansion (no expansion)
License Hach's technology to consumer brands or partner with consumer companies to create co‑branded products

X1.name: Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Home Water Test Kits
X1.method: Online survey with a sample of homeowners and renters in regions with varying water quality regulations. Participants are offered a mock premium test kit at two price points: $20 (one-time test) and $40 (reusable strips and accessories). They are asked: (1) How likely are they to purchase the kit? (2) What would be the maximum price they would pay for a reusable version? (3) Why would they choose to purchase? (open-ended).
X1.sample: 500 respondents (200 in regions with strict water quality laws, 200 in regions with moderate laws, 100 in regions with few regulations). Recruit via online panels to match demographic distribution.
X1.measure: Share of respondents indicating "high" likelihood to purchase at each price point, plus average maximum price willingness to pay for a reusable version.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher willingness to pay and purchase intent at the $40 price point than at $20, especially in regions with strict regulations.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Purchase intent and willingness to pay are similar across price points and do not differ by regulatory region.

X1.decision_rule: If the share of respondents indicating "high" likelihood to purchase at $40 exceeds 30% and exceeds the share at $20 by at least 5 percentage points, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on peace-of-mind monitoring. If the difference is less than 5 percentage points, consider a lower-priced entry product or maintain B2B focus. If neither condition is met, do not invest in a consumer proposition.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a warehouse label printer and packing errors, which does not address consumer demand, willingness to pay, or regulatory requirements for home water test kits. Therefore it provides no support or contradiction to T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Public evidence shows home water test kits are widely available and sold under Hach brands, but it does not demonstrate consumer demand, willingness to pay, or regulatory requirement. Conduct the proposed willingness-to-pay survey to test T1 vs. T2 before committing resources.
final.target_customer: Individual homeowners and renters who are concerned about water quality but currently rely on utility or professional testing.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition that provides peace-of-mind monitoring of drinking water quality through a premium test kit and accessories, leveraging Hach’s existing brand credibility and distribution.
final.next_action: Run the 12‑week, €12,000 willingness-to-pay survey with 500 respondents to measure purchase intent and price sensitivity at two price points.
final.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market, actual purchase intent, willingness to pay for a premium product, and the extent to which regulatory requirements drive demand remain uncertain.
would_change_if: If the survey shows purchase intent at $40 exceeds 30% and is at least 5 percentage points higher than at $20, indicating strong demand for peace-of-mind monitoring.
If new evidence shows that regulatory bodies in target regions actively require DIY water testing, supporting T2.

X1.name: Digital Messaging Test for Home Water Testing Kit
X1.method: Run a targeted digital ad campaign offering a free, limited-edition home water test kit (containing 5 tests: lead, copper, chlorine, pH, and alkalinity) to homeowners in regions with known water quality concerns. Ads will be served to users who have shown interest in home improvement or water quality topics. Track click-through rate (CTR) and conversion rate (purchases).
X1.sample: Estimated 5,000 unique visitors per ad (10,000 total impressions) across 3 regions (e.g., California, Florida, Texas) with varying water quality concerns.
X1.measure: Conversion rate: percentage of visitors who purchase the test kit after clicking the ad.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Conversion rate will be above 5% in all regions, indicating consumer demand for peace-of-mind monitoring.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Conversion rate will be above 5% only in regions with strict water quality regulations (e.g., California, Texas) and below 5% in other regions, indicating regulatory-driven demand.

X1.decision_rule: If the average conversion rate across all regions is above 5%, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If conversion rates are below 5% in at least two regions, conclude that consumer demand is insufficient and recommend maintaining the B2B focus.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a warehouse label printer and packing errors, which does not address consumer demand for home water testing kits. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners concerned about water quality, leveraging the existing AquaChek brand and distribution channels. Begin with a limited launch of a premium test kit (5 tests) marketed as a peace-of-mind solution, and collect purchase data to validate demand.
final.target_customer: Individual homeowners and renters in regions with known water quality concerns (e.g., areas with lead, copper, or other contaminants) who currently rely on utility or professional testing.
final.value_proposition: Provide an independent, at-home water quality test that offers peace of mind and control over drinking water, with the confidence of a trusted brand and the convenience of a single-use kit.
final.next_action: Run the proposed digital messaging test (5,000 visitors, 3 regions) to measure conversion rates and decide on a full launch based on the 5% threshold.
final.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market and actual purchase intent are unknown; the test will determine whether demand is sufficient to justify investment.
would_change_if: If the digital test shows conversion rates below 5% in at least two regions, indicating insufficient consumer demand, the recommendation would shift to maintain the B2B focus.
If new evidence shows strong regulatory demand in specific regions, the theory would shift toward T2 and the recommendation would change to prioritize compliance-focused sales.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing home dishwasher ownership and increased awareness of hygiene make consumers seek reliable, premium equipment for home use.

assumptions: Homeowners are willing to pay a premium for German-made, low-operating-cost dishwashers.
Winterhalter can reach homeowners through existing distribution channels or new direct sales channels.
Consumer demand for hygiene and compact design is sufficient to justify a differentiated home proposition.
predictions: A survey of homeowners shows at least 30% would purchase a Winterhalter home dishwasher at a price 15% above standard models.

assumptions: Small restaurants and hotels are willing to invest in compact, high-efficiency dishwashers.

The demand for compact warewashing in small kitchens is sufficient to justify a differentiated consumer proposition.
predictions: A survey of small restaurants shows at least 40% would purchase a compact Winterhalter dishwasher at a price 10% below standard models.

X1.name: Homeowner Purchase Intent Pilot
X1.method: Online survey with a controlled offer. Participants are recruited from homeowners who have completed a kitchen survey. They are randomly assigned to one of two treatment groups: Group A (customisable model) and Group B (professional-grade model). Both groups see a product description of a Winterhalter undercounter dishwasher with a price point 20% above a standard model. Group A also receives a customisation option and a discount for adding a glassware kit. Participants indicate their willingness to pay (WTP) and likelihood to purchase on a 7-point scale.
X1.sample: 300 homeowners recruited via an online panel, 150 per group, balanced for age, income, and kitchen ownership status
X1.measure: Average WTP (in euros) and purchase intent (on 7-point scale) for each group

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show higher average WTP and purchase intent than Group B, because homeowners value customisation and premium pricing.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show higher average WTP and purchase intent than Group A, because homeowners seek a professional-grade, hygienic solution.

X1.decision_rule: If Group A's average WTP is at least 20% higher than Group B's and the difference is statistically significant (p<0.05), we conclude T1 is supported and recommend developing a differentiated consumer proposition focused on customisation and premium pricing. If Group B's average WTP is at least 20% higher than Group A and the difference is statistically significant, we conclude T2 is supported and recommend a professional-grade consumer proposition. If neither difference is statistically significant, we conclude neither theory is strongly supported and recommend no new consumer proposition at this time.

arguments.name: Homeowner Purchase Intent Pilot
arguments.method: Online survey with a controlled offer. Participants are recruited from homeowners who have completed a kitchen survey. They are randomly assigned to one of two treatment groups: Group A (customisable model) and Group B (professional-grade model). Both groups see a product description of a Winterhalter undercounter dishwasher with a price point 20% above a standard model. Group A also receives a customisation option and a discount for adding a glassware kit. Participants indicate their willingness to pay (WTP) and likelihood to purchase on a 7-point scale.
arguments.sample: 300 homeowners recruited via an online panel, 150 per group, balanced for age, income, and kitchen ownership status
arguments.measure: Average WTP (in euros) and purchase intent (on 7-point scale) for each group

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show higher average WTP and purchase intent than Group B, because homeowners value customisation and premium pricing.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show higher average WTP and purchase intent than Group A, because homeowners seek a professional-grade, hygienic solution.

arguments.decision_rule: If Group A's average WTP is at least 20% higher than Group B's and the difference is statistically significant (p<0.05), we conclude T1 is supported and recommend developing a differentiated consumer proposition focused on customisation and premium pricing. If Group B's average WTP is at least 20% higher than Group A and the difference is statistically significant, we conclude T2 is supported and recommend a professional-grade consumer proposition. If neither difference is statistically significant, we conclude neither theory is strongly supported and recommend no new consumer proposition at this time.

Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment
Must consider Franke’s existing professional offerings (fully automatic, semi-automatic, traditional) and its current consumer reach
Must assess demand, competitive landscape, and potential value capture mechanisms
alternatives: Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home office, small retail, travel) with a new product or service model
Expand the existing professional line into adjacent consumer segments without a new differentiated proposition (e.g., add consumer accessories, subscription services, or new distribution channels)
Maintain current product portfolio and focus on existing professional market; no expansion
License Franke’s technology or brand to third‑party consumer product manufacturers rather than creating a direct consumer proposition

T1.claim: Home office consumers will adopt Franke coffee machines because they value professional-grade, high-quality coffee and are willing to pay a premium for reliability and consistency, leading to repeat purchases and brand loyalty.
T1.who_benefits: Home office professionals and small business owners who need a reliable coffee solution for their workspace.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: These consumers perceive professional coffee machines as a status symbol and a necessity for productivity, unlike generic consumer machines that may produce inconsistent results.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Franke can capture value through premium pricing, subscription services for maintenance and service, and direct-to-consumer sales channels that emphasize quality and professional features.
assumptions: Home office consumers are willing to invest in professional-grade coffee equipment.
Franke's brand perception of quality translates into consumer purchase decisions.
The market size for home office coffee machines is sufficient to justify a differentiated proposition.
predictions: Surveyed home office consumers will indicate a willingness to pay at least 20% more for a Franke machine compared to a comparable consumer brand.
Purchase intent for Franke will be higher among consumers who cite professional quality as a primary reason.
Repeat purchase rate for Franke will be higher than for generic consumer machines.
T1.first_claim: Home office consumers will adopt Franke coffee machines because they value professional-grade, high-quality coffee and are willing to pay a premium for reliability and consistency, leading to repeat purchases and brand loyalty.

T2.claim: Home office consumers will adopt Franke coffee machines because they value convenience and ease of use, and are willing to pay for machines that require minimal maintenance and offer quick brewing, leading to higher adoption rates.
T2.who_benefits: Home office professionals who need a coffee solution that is easy to operate and maintain, reducing time spent on coffee preparation.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: These consumers prioritize convenience and efficiency, especially in busy work environments where time is limited. They are less concerned with professional-grade quality and more focused on the simplicity of use.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Franke can capture value through lower upfront costs, bundled maintenance services, and marketing that emphasizes ease of use and quick brewing, potentially attracting a broader consumer base.
assumptions: Home office consumers are willing to pay a premium for convenience and ease of use.
Franke's existing professional reputation does not deter consumers from choosing a consumer product.
The market size for convenience-focused coffee machines is sufficient to justify a differentiated proposition.
predictions: Surveyed home office consumers will rank convenience and ease of use as the top two reasons for choosing a coffee machine.
Purchase intent for Franke will be higher among consumers who cite convenience as a primary reason.
Repeat purchase rate for Franke will be comparable to or higher than for consumer brands that emphasize convenience.

X1.name: Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Home Office Coffee Machines
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.
X1.sample: 500 home office professionals (self-identified) recruited via a panel, balanced for region and industry.
X1.measure: Average WTP in euros for a Franke consumer machine (e.g., A300) compared to a comparable consumer brand (e.g., De'Longhi).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Home office consumers will report a WTP at least 20% higher for Franke than for the comparable consumer brand, with professional quality cited as the primary reason.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Home office consumers will report a WTP at least 20% higher for Franke than for the comparable consumer brand, with convenience and ease of use cited as the primary reason.

X1.decision_rule: If the average WTP for Franke exceeds the WTP for the comparable consumer brand by at least 20% across both theories, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 20% or neither theory is supported, do not invest.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting home office professionals who value professional-grade coffee quality and reliability. Begin with a willingness-to-pay survey to validate demand before committing to product development.
final.target_customer: Home office professionals and small business owners who need a reliable, high-quality coffee solution for their workspace.
final.value_proposition: A Franke consumer machine that emphasizes professional-grade quality, consistency, and reliability, positioned as a premium product for home office environments.
final.next_action: Run the proposed willingness-to-pay survey (500 home office professionals, 8 weeks, €15,000) to measure actual willingness to pay for a Franke consumer machine versus a comparable consumer brand.
final.uncertainty: The size of the home office market and the actual willingness to pay a premium for professional-grade coffee are uncertain. Evidence from the survey will resolve whether T1 is supported.
would_change_if: If the survey shows a willingness-to-pay difference of less than 20% between Franke and a comparable consumer brand, indicating insufficient demand for a premium proposition.
If new public evidence shows strong consumer demand for convenience and ease of use, shifting the focus toward T2.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting home office and small retail segments, emphasizing professional-grade coffee quality and brand prestige. Begin with a limited pilot to test willingness to pay and purchase intent before full-scale development.

frame.objective: Determine whether Franke Coffee Systems should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its professional coffee machines, and identify what public evidence would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment
Must consider Franke’s existing professional offerings (fully automatic, semi-automatic, traditional) and its current consumer reach
Must assess demand, competitive landscape, and potential value capture mechanisms
alternatives: Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home office, small retail, travel) with a new product or service model
Expand the existing professional line into adjacent consumer segments without a new differentiated proposition (e.g., add consumer accessories, subscription services, or new distribution channels)
Maintain current product portfolio and focus on existing professional market; no expansion
License Franke’s technology or brand to third‑party consumer product manufacturers rather than creating a direct consumer proposition

T1.claim: Home office and small retail consumers will adopt a differentiated Franke consumer product because they value professional-grade coffee quality and brand reputation, and they are willing to pay a premium for a machine that delivers consistent, high-quality coffee.
T1.who_benefits: Home office professionals and small retailers who need reliable, high-quality coffee for their customers or themselves.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: These consumers perceive professional coffee machines as a status symbol and a quality differentiator, leading them to choose a brand that signals reliability and premium quality over generic options.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Franke can capture value through premium pricing, direct-to-consumer sales, and brand positioning as a premium coffee solution, potentially commanding higher margins than its professional line.
assumptions: Consumers associate professional-grade coffee with higher quality and brand prestige.
There is sufficient demand in home office and small retail segments to justify a differentiated product.
Franke's brand recognition and reputation can be leveraged to justify premium pricing.
predictions: Consumers will express willingness to pay at least 20% more for a Franke consumer machine compared to a comparable entry-level consumer machine.
Surveyed home office professionals will rank coffee quality as the top factor in purchasing decisions for a new coffee machine.
Sales of a differentiated consumer product will be higher in regions where professional coffee culture is strong.

T2.who_benefits: Home office professionals and small retailers who need a consistent, easy-to-operate coffee machine that fits their limited space and budget.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: These consumers prioritize convenience and reliability over brand prestige, seeking a machine that requires minimal maintenance and integrates seamlessly into their workflow, reducing the hassle of managing multiple devices.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Franke can capture value through lower unit costs, simplified product design, and potentially lower pricing, allowing higher volume sales and reduced distribution complexity.
assumptions: Consumers value convenience and reliability over brand prestige.
There is sufficient demand in home office and small retail segments for a single, easy-to-use coffee machine.
Franke's existing product line can be adapted to meet these convenience requirements without significant redesign.
predictions: Consumers will choose a Franke consumer machine over multiple entry-level devices due to perceived convenience.
Surveyed home office professionals will rank ease of use and low maintenance as the top factors in purchasing decisions.
Sales of a differentiated consumer product will be higher in regions where space and budget constraints are significant.

X1.name: Product Messaging Test: Premium vs Convenience Framing
X1.method: Online survey with targeted recruitment of home office professionals and small retailers. Participants view one of two product descriptions for a Franke consumer machine (A300 or Mythos). Description A emphasizes professional-grade coffee quality, brand prestige, and suitability for modern workspaces. Description B emphasizes convenience, low maintenance, and space efficiency. Participants then indicate their willingness to pay (WTP) and likelihood to purchase on a 7-point scale (1‑2 ).
X1.sample: 400 respondents (200 per condition) recruited via professional networking sites and retail forums to ensure target demographics.
X1.measure: Average WTP (eur) and purchase intent (7-point scale) for each condition.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Premium condition will achieve higher average WTP and purchase intent than convenience condition, indicating demand for quality-driven pricing.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Convenience condition will achieve higher average WTP and purchase intent than premium condition, indicating demand for low-maintenance, space‑friendly solutions.

X1.decision_rule: If premium condition average WTP ≥ €80 and exceeds convenience condition by at least 15 points, proceed to develop a premium consumer proposition. If convenience condition average WTP ≥ €80 and exceeds premium condition by at least 15 points, focus on a convenience‑driven proposition. If neither condition meets its threshold, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer reducing packing errors and does not address consumer demand for premium quality or convenience. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting home office and small retail segments, emphasizing professional-grade coffee quality and brand prestige. Begin with a limited pilot to test willingness to pay and purchase intent before full-scale development.
final.target_customer: Home office professionals and small retailers who need reliable, high-quality coffee for their customers or themselves.
final.value_proposition: A Franke consumer machine that delivers professional-grade coffee quality, brand reputation, and consistent performance, positioned as a premium solution for modern workspaces.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Product Messaging Test (premium vs convenience framing) to validate demand for quality-driven pricing. If the premium condition meets the willingness-to-pay threshold, proceed to develop a premium consumer line; otherwise,
final.uncertainty: The exact size of the consumer market and willingness to pay for premium quality are uncertain. Evidence from the test will resolve whether demand is sufficient to justify investment.
would_change_if: If the test shows the convenience condition achieving a higher willingness-to-pay threshold, the recommendation would shift to a convenience-driven proposition.
If new public evidence demonstrates strong consumer demand for low-maintenance, space-friendly machines, the recommendation would shift accordingly.

frame.objective: Determine whether Franke Coffee Systems should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its professional coffee machines, and identify what public evidence would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available

Must assess demand, competitive landscape, and potential value capture mechanisms
alternatives: Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home office, small retail, travel) with a new product or service model

License Franke’s technology or brand to third‑party consumer product manufacturers rather than creating a direct consumer proposition

T1.claim: Home office workers will adopt a differentiated Franke consumer proposition because they need reliable, high-quality coffee for remote work and value a machine that integrates with their workflow and can be managed remotely.
T1.who_benefits: Home office workers and their employers who need consistent coffee quality and convenience.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: The rise of remote work has increased demand for coffee machines that can be controlled and monitored from anywhere, reducing the need for on-site staff and improving productivity.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Franke can capture value by selling a smart, connected machine with remote management features at a premium price, leveraging its professional reputation to signal quality and reliability.
assumptions: Home office workers are willing to pay a premium for a machine that can be controlled remotely.
Remote management features are a significant differentiator for this segment.
Franke can develop and market a product that meets these requirements.
predictions: A survey of home office workers will show a higher willingness to purchase a smart, connected Franke machine compared to a standard consumer machine.
Pilot sales of the smart machine will show higher conversion rates among home office users than among general consumers.
Customers will report higher satisfaction with remote control and monitoring features.
T1.first_claim: Home office workers will adopt a differentiated Franke consumer proposition because they need reliable, high-quality coffee for remote work and value a machine that integrates with their workflow and can be managed remotely.

T2.claim: Home consumers will adopt a differentiated Franke consumer proposition because they value a machine that offers superior coffee quality and convenience, and are willing to pay a premium for a product that delivers consistent, high-quality coffee.
T2.who_benefits: Home consumers who prioritize coffee quality and convenience in their daily routine.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers are increasingly seeking products that deliver superior taste and convenience, and are willing to pay more for a machine that meets these expectations.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Franke can capture value by positioning its machines as premium, high-quality products and charging a premium price, leveraging its professional reputation to signal quality.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a machine that delivers superior coffee quality.
The premium price is justified by the perceived quality and convenience.
Franke can effectively communicate the quality benefits to consumers.
predictions: A survey of home consumers will show a higher willingness to purchase a premium-priced Franke machine compared to a standard consumer machine.
Pilot sales of the premium-priced machine will show higher conversion rates among quality-conscious consumers than among general consumers.
Customers will report higher satisfaction with the overall coffee experience when using the premium-priced machine.
T2.first_claim: Home consumers will adopt a differentiated Franke consumer proposition because they value a machine that offers superior coffee quality and convenience, and are willing to pay a premium for a product that delivers consistent, high-quality coffee.
