frame.objective: Determine whether Franke Coffee Systems should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its professional coffee machines, and identify what public evidence would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment
Must consider Franke’s existing professional offerings (fully automatic, semi-automatic, traditional) and its current consumer reach
Must assess demand, competitive landscape, and potential value capture mechanisms
alternatives: Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home office, small retail, travel) with a new product or service model
Expand the existing professional line into adjacent consumer segments without a new differentiated proposition (e.g., add consumer accessories, subscription services, or new distribution channels)
Maintain current product portfolio and focus on existing professional market; no expansion
License Franke’s technology or brand to third‑party consumer product manufacturers rather than creating a direct consumer proposition

T1.claim: Home office consumers will adopt a differentiated Franke coffee machine if they perceive it as a status symbol that signals professionalism and reliability, because they value brand prestige and are willing to pay a premium for it.
T1.who_benefits: Franke Coffee Systems (through higher margins on premium-priced machines) and early adopters of the brand who seek to project professionalism.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers shift from utilitarian purchase decisions to status-driven purchases when a product is framed as a premium, professional-grade item rather than a basic household appliance.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Franke can price the machine at a premium, sell through dedicated consumer channels, and capture value through brand loyalty and repeat purchases.
assumptions: Consumers associate professional coffee machines with higher quality and brand prestige.
Status signaling is a significant driver of purchase decisions for home office users.
Franke can effectively communicate this status proposition to its target audience.
predictions: Surveyed home office users will indicate that brand prestige is a top factor in choosing a coffee machine.
Willingness to pay for a premium-priced Franke machine will be higher than for comparable non-branded machines.
Sales of a differentiated Franke machine will be concentrated among users who already own professional-grade coffee equipment.
T1.first_claim: Home office consumers will adopt a differentiated Franke coffee machine if they perceive it as a status symbol that signals professionalism and reliability, because they value brand prestige and are willing to pay a premium for it.

T2.claim: Home office consumers will adopt a differentiated Franke coffee machine if they need a reliable, high-quality coffee solution that reduces daily coffee preparation time, because they value efficiency and consistency in their work environment.
T2.who_benefits: Franke Coffee Systems (through increased volume sales and repeat purchases of replacement parts and consumables) and early adopters who seek to streamline their coffee routine.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers shift from utilitarian purchase decisions to efficiency-driven purchases when a product offers faster, more consistent coffee preparation, reducing the time spent on daily coffee tasks.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Franke can capture value through higher unit volume sales, recurring revenue from consumables, and potential partnerships with coffee shop chains or service providers to offer maintenance packages.
assumptions: Consumers prioritize coffee quality and consistency over brand prestige.
Time savings are a significant purchase driver for home office users.
Franke can demonstrate measurable time savings in product demonstrations or trials.
predictions: Home office users will rank time savings as a top factor in choosing a coffee machine.
Willingness to pay for a machine that reduces coffee preparation time will be higher than for a machine with similar features but no time-saving claim.
Sales of a differentiated Franke machine will be concentrated among users who already own multiple coffee machines and seek to optimize their workflow.

X1.name: Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Differentiated Consumer Ice Machine
X1.method: Online survey with a choice-based conjoint design. Participants are recruited from residential households in Japan. They view a mock Hoshizaki countertop ice machine with three variants: a standard compact model, a premium-priced energy-efficient model, and a basic model. Each variant is described with features such as energy rating, brand reputation, and price. Participants indicate their maximum price they would pay for each variant and whether they would purchase it.
X1.sample: Proposed sample: 400 Japanese residential households (200 per variant) recruited via an online panel. Recruitment target: households with at least one adult member aged 18-65 who makes purchasing decisions for home appliances.
X1.measure: Primary measure: average maximum price participants indicate they would pay for each variant. Secondary measure: binary purchase intent (would buy) for each variant.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Average maximum price for the standard compact variant will be the highest, and purchase intent will be low across all variants.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Average maximum price for the premium-priced variant will be the highest, and purchase intent will be low across all variants.

X1.decision_rule: If the average maximum price for the premium-priced variant exceeds the average maximum price for the standard compact variant by at least 15% (e.g., premium price ≥ 1.15 × standard price), conclude T2 is supported and recommend a premium-priced consumer proposition. If the premium price does not exceed the standard price by 15% or if purchase intent for the premium variant is low, conclude T1 is supported and recommend a convenience-focused consumer proposition. If neither condition is met, suggest further market research.

final.next_action: Run the proposed willingness-to-pay survey (400 Japanese households, 8 weeks, €18,000) to measure maximum price and purchase intent for three variants: standard compact, premium-priced energy-efficient, and basic. Use the 15% price premium

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and WTP for the premium-priced unit than for the eco-friendly unit
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and WTP for the eco-friendly unit than for the premium-priced unit

final.next_action: Run the proposed 8‑week, €18,000 willingness-to-pay survey with randomized messaging to measure purchase intent and price sensitivity against a standard commercial unit.
final.uncertainty: Actual consumer willingness to pay a premium for convenience and the size of the residential market; Hoshizaki’s ability to produce a compact, energy-efficient unit; competitive response from existing consumer ice machine brands.
would_change_if: If the survey shows purchase intent below 15% or willingness to pay below $400, the investment would be reconsidered in favor of maintaining the commercial focus

T1.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers shift from a one-time purchase to repeat purchases when they experience a clear return on investment (e.g., reduced cleaning time, lower water usage, or increased surface longevity).
T1.how_value_is_captured: Tennant would capture value through premium pricing, subscription-based maintenance services, and data-driven upsell opportunities (e.g., suggesting accessories or upgrades).

Regulatory and safety standards allow consumer-grade products to be marketed as premium solutions.

X1.name: Premium vs Sustainability Messaging Test
X1.method: Recruit a sample of homeowners and small business owners interested in cleaning equipment. Randomly assign participants to two equal groups: Group A receives a premium-priced walk-behind scrubber marketed as 'convenience-enabled' (highlighting time savings and simple operation). Group B receives the same product marketed as 'water‑saving' and 'chemical‑free' (highlighting sustainability). Both groups view product specifications and price. After viewing, participants indicate purchase intent (binary: would buy) and maximum price they would pay.
X1.sample: 200 participants (100 per group), recruited via online panels targeting homeowners and small businesses in the United States and Western Europe.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary) and maximum price willingness to pay for each group.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show purchase intent at least 15% higher than Group B.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show purchase intent at least 15% higher than Group A.

X1.decision_rule: If Group A’s purchase intent is at least 15% higher than Group B’s, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on convenience. If Group B’s purchase intent is at least 15% higher, develop a differentiated proposition focused on sustainability. If neither threshold is met, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Public evidence shows Tennant already sells consumer-grade products (e.g., wet/dry vacuums, high-pressure washers) and has a consumer channel, but it does not demonstrate consumer willingness to pay a premium for convenience or sustainability. final.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition that positions the product as a premium, convenience-enabled solution offering measurable time or cost savings, supported by clear return-on-investment messaging.
final.next_action: Run the Premium vs Sustainability Messaging Test (200 participants, 12 weeks, €20,000 budget) to determine whether purchase intent for convenience messaging exceeds that for sustainability messaging.
final.uncertainty: The evidence does not show consumer willingness to pay a premium for convenience or sustainability, nor does it quantify demand for a differentiated proposition. The test results will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the Premium Messaging Test shows purchase intent at least 15% higher than Sustainability Messaging, we would proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on convenience.
If the Sustainability Messaging Test shows purchase intent at least 15% higher than Premium Messaging, we would develop a differentiated proposition focused on sustainability.
If neither test meets its threshold, we would maintain the current B2B focus and not pursue consumer expansion.

X1.name: Consumer Proposition Test: Premium vs. Sustainable Messaging
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer and product description. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Premium Condition (emphasizes convenience, time savings, and ease of use) or Sustainable Condition (emphasizes water-saving, chemical-free, and eco-friendly features). Both conditions present the same consumer-grade walk-behind scrubber at a fixed price point (e.g., €300). Participants indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and willingness to pay a premium (additional €20).
X1.sample: 500 adults in the United States, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and income to reflect a typical consumer segment.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (percentage of participants indicating "very likely" to purchase) and willingness to pay a premium (difference in additional €20 willingness to pay between Premium and Sustainable conditions).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Premium Condition will achieve purchase intent at least 15% higher than Sustainable Condition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Sustainable Condition will achieve purchase intent at least 15% higher than Premium Condition.

If Sustainable Condition's purchase intent exceeds Premium Condition's by at least 15 percentage points, recommend a sustainable consumer proposition. If neither condition exceeds the 15‑point threshold, recommend no expansion into consumer markets.

final.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes convenience, performance, and ease of use, positioned as a premium, time-saving solution for home and small‑business cleaning tasks.
final.next_action: Run the Consumer Proposition Test (Premium vs. Sustainable messaging) to validate purchase intent and willingness to pay before committing resources.
final.uncertainty: Consumer willingness to pay a premium for cleaning equipment and the specific demand drivers (convenience vs. sustainability) remain uncertain. The test will resolve these uncertainties.
would_change_if: If the Premium Condition's purchase intent exceeds the Sustainable Condition's by at least 15 percentage points, we would recommend developing a differentiated consumer proposition focused on convenience and performance.

X1.name: Premium vs. Eco-Premium Consumer Scrubber Test
X1.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants view a product description of a consumer-grade walk-behind scrubber (identical performance spec but marketed differently). One version is marketed as a premium convenience product (e.g., 'Save time with smart cleaning technology') and the other as an eco‑premium product (e.g., 'Water‑saving and chemical‑free cleaning solution'). Both versions are priced at a 20% premium over a comparable professional model. Participants indicate purchase intent (1‑7 scale) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR).
X1.sample: 300 adult consumers in the US and Western Europe, screened for interest in home cleaning and willingness to pay a premium for cleaning equipment.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (1‑7 scale) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR). Secondary measure: stated importance of convenience vs. sustainability.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Premium version will achieve purchase intent at least 15% higher and higher willingness to pay than eco‑premium version.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Eco‑premium version will achieve purchase intent at least 15% higher and higher willingness to pay than premium version.

X1.decision_rule: If premium version purchase intent ≥ 15% points higher than eco‑premium version AND premium willingness to pay ≥ 20% higher than eco‑premium willingness to pay, proceed to develop a premium consumer proposition. If eco‑premium version ≥ 15% points higher, develop an eco‑premium proposition. If neither threshold is met, do not expand into consumer market.

final.recommendation: Do not yet commit to a full consumer proposition. Conduct the proposed premium vs. eco‑premium conjoint test to measure actual purchase intent and willingness to pay. If the premium version meets the 15‑point threshold, proceed to develop a premium consumer proposition; if the eco‑premium version meets the threshold, develop an eco‑premium proposition. If neither meets the threshold, maintain the current B2B focus.
final.target_customer: Homeowners and small business owners who currently struggle with traditional cleaning methods or lack the expertise to maintain surfaces effectively.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer product that delivers superior cleaning performance at an economical price point, marketed as either a premium convenience solution or an eco‑premium sustainable product, with potential for subscription services.
final.next_action: Run the 8‑week, €18,000 conjoint test with 300 US/Western European consumers, comparing premium convenience vs. eco‑premium messaging.
final.uncertainty: Consumer willingness to pay a premium for cleaning equipment and the relative importance of convenience versus sustainability are uncertain. The test will resolve these uncertainties.
would_change_if: If the premium version fails to achieve the 15‑point purchase intent threshold, we would abandon the consumer expansion and focus on the existing B2B segment.
If the eco‑premium version fails to achieve the 15‑point threshold, we would abandon the eco‑premium proposition and focus on premium convenience.
If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for a specific use case (e.g., pet‑friendly cleaning) that is not currently served, we would reconsider the consumer proposition.

arguments.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants view a product description of a consumer-grade walk-behind scrubber (identical performance spec but marketed differently). One version is marketed as a premium convenience product (e.g., 'Save time with smart cleaning technology') and the other as an eco‑premium product (e.g., 'Water‑saving and chemical‑free cleaning solution'). Both versions are priced at a 20% premium over a comparable professional model. Participants indicate purchase intent (1‑7 scale) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR).
arguments.sample: 300 adult consumers in the US and Western Europe, screened for interest in home cleaning and willingness to pay a premium for cleaning equipment.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (1‑7 scale) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR). Secondary measure: stated importance of convenience vs. sustainability.

arguments.decision_rule: If premium version purchase intent ≥ 15% points higher than eco‑premium version AND premium willingness to pay ≥ 20% higher than eco‑premium willingness to pay, proceed to develop a premium consumer proposition. frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Tennant investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its professional floor-cleaning machines, and identify what evidence would support that investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment
Must distinguish demand from capability, and consider distribution and regulatory hurdles
Must consider existing consumer reach (direct vs distributor channels) and any potential competitive landscape
alternatives: Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home cleaning, small‑business janitorial, or a niche like pet‑friendly cleaning)
Expand the existing professional line into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add consumer‑grade features to existing models)
Maintain the current B2B focus and not pursue consumer expansion (no expansion)
License the professional technology to consumer brands rather than selling under Tennant's own consumer brand

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive the product as a premium, convenience-enabled solution that simplifies cleaning tasks and offers measurable time or cost savings.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners and small business owners who currently struggle with traditional cleaning methods or lack the expertise to maintain surfaces effectively.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers shift from a one-time purchase to repeat purchases when they experience a clear return on investment (e.g., reduced cleaning time, lower water usage, or increased surface longevity).
T1.how_value_is_captured: Tennant would capture value through premium pricing, subscription-based maintenance services, and data-driven upsell opportunities (e.g., suggesting accessories or upgrades).
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for convenience and performance.
The product can be distributed through existing retail channels without significant logistical changes.
Regulatory and safety standards allow consumer-grade products to be marketed as premium solutions.
predictions: In a test offering a consumer-grade walk-behind scrubber at a 20% premium over a comparable professional model, purchase intent will be at least 15% higher than a baseline offer at the same price point.
Repeat purchase rate (e.g., repeat purchase within 12 months) will be at least 10% higher for the premium product compared to a standard professional model.

T2.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers shift from a one-time purchase to repeat purchases when they experience a clear environmental benefit (e.g., lower water usage, reduced chemical exposure, or carbon footprint reduction).
T2.how_value_is_captured: Tennant would capture value through premium pricing justified by sustainability credentials, partnerships with eco-friendly brands, and potential government incentives for green products.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for sustainable products.
The product can be marketed as eco-friendly without compromising performance.
Regulatory frameworks support eco-friendly cleaning product labeling and certification.
predictions: In a test offering a consumer-grade scrubber marketed as 'water‑saving' and 'chemical‑free', purchase intent will be at least 15% higher than a baseline offer at the same price point.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Tennant investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its professional floor-cleaning machines, and identify what evidence would support that investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive the product as a premium, convenience-enabled solution that simplifies cleaning tasks and offers measurable time or cost savings.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners and small business owners who currently struggle with traditional cleaning methods or lack the expertise to maintain surfaces effectively.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers shift from a one-time purchase to repeat purchases when they experience a clear return on investment (e.g., reduced cleaning time, lower water usage, or increased surface longevity).
T1.how_value_is_captured: Tennant would capture value through premium pricing, subscription-based maintenance services, and data-driven upsell opportunities (e.g., suggesting accessories or upgrades).
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for convenience and performance.
The product can be distributed through existing retail channels without significant logistical changes.
Regulatory and safety standards allow consumer-grade products to be marketed as premium solutions.
predictions: In a test offering a consumer-grade walk-behind scrubber at a 20% premium over a comparable professional model, purchase intent will be at least 15% higher than a baseline offer at the same price point.

X1.method: Online survey with two distinct scenarios presented to homeowners. Scenario A presents a Belimo smart thermostat with a premium price (e.g., €300) and emphasizes energy savings and smart home integration. Scenario B presents the same product at a lower price (e.g., €150) and emphasizes long-term cost savings and reduced maintenance. Participants indicate their maximum price they would pay for each scenario.
X1.sample: 400 U.S. homeowners who have central air conditioning and own a programmable thermostat, recruited via an online panel. Stratify by household income to reflect diverse economic profiles.
X1.measure: Maximum price participants would pay for Scenario A (premium version) and Scenario B (cost-saving version).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Participants will indicate a higher maximum price for Scenario A than for Scenario B, indicating willingness to pay a premium for energy savings and smart home integration.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Participants will indicate a higher maximum price for Scenario B than for Scenario A, indicating willingness to pay a lower price for long-term cost savings.

X1.decision_rule: If the average maximum price for Scenario A exceeds Scenario B by at least €50, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing premium features (T1). arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.
arguments.sample: 400 U.S. homeowners who currently own central air conditioning and have a programmable thermostat, recruited via an online panel.
arguments.measure: Average WTP in euros for a Belimo smart thermostat with integrated zone control and smart home integration, and self-reported primary purchase motivation (premium, cost savings, or other).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Homeowners will report WTP at least €150 for the smart thermostat, citing premium features and smart home integration as the primary reason.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Homeowners will report WTP at least €200 for the smart thermostat, citing annual energy savings and reduced maintenance costs as the primary reason.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average WTP for T1 exceeds €150 and the proportion of respondents citing premium features as the primary reason is at least 40%, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on premium features. If the average WTP for T2 exceeds €200 and the proportion of respondents citing cost savings as the primary reason is at least 40%, consider a cost‑saving‑focused proposition. If neither threshold is met, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.

X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging to test two value propositions: premium energy‑saving upgrade vs. cost‑saving long‑term investment.

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 30% of respondents will indicate intent to purchase if framed as a premium, energy‑saving upgrade; willingness to pay will be above €300.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Public evidence shows Belimo already offers residential HVAC actuators (Belimo Achr Residential 2015) and provides OEM support for residential HVAC projects (Belimo OEM Integrators 2025), but no source shows consumer willingness to pay a premium for Belimo's specific smart actuators or actual purchase intent. frame.objective: Determine whether Belimo Holding AG should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current HVAC actuators, valves, and sensors, and identify what public evidence would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment
Must consider Belimo’s existing B2B focus and current consumer reach
Any recommendation must be based on evidence of demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage
alternatives: Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home energy management, smart home integration)
Expand into adjacent B2B segments (e.g., industrial automation, renewable energy) with a consumer-facing offering
Maintain current B2B focus and not pursue consumer expansion
License Belimo’s technology to consumer brands rather than selling under Belimo’s own brand

T1.claim: Homeowners will adopt Belimo residential smart HVAC products if they perceive them as a premium, energy‑saving upgrade that offers precise temperature control and integration with existing smart home ecosystems.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners seeking comfort and energy savings; Belimo gains premium pricing and brand differentiation.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing awareness of energy costs and smart home convenience motivates homeowners to replace traditional thermostats with smart, programmable devices.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Belimo can charge a premium price for its integrated smart actuators and valves, leveraging its existing OEM relationships to reach consumers through retail or direct channels.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for energy‑efficient, smart HVAC solutions.
Belimo can scale production and distribution to meet consumer demand without compromising B2B relationships.
Smart home integration capabilities are technically feasible and accepted by homeowners.
predictions: A survey of homeowners would show at least 30% indicating intent to purchase a Belimo smart thermostat within the next 12 months.
Sales of Belimo residential smart actuators would increase in regions with higher energy‑cost awareness.
Competitor smart thermostat offerings would not significantly erode Belimo's market share in the residential segment.
T1.first_claim: Homeowners will adopt Belimo residential smart HVAC products if they perceive them as a premium, energy‑saving upgrade that offers precise temperature control and integration with existing smart home ecosystems.

T2.claim: Homeowners will adopt Belimo residential smart HVAC products if they perceive them as a cost‑saving, long‑term investment that reduces energy bills and maintenance needs, rather than as a premium lifestyle upgrade.
T2.who_benefits: Homeowners focused on long‑term cost savings and lower maintenance; Belimo gains recurring revenue and brand loyalty.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Economic uncertainty and rising energy costs make homeowners seek solutions that directly lower monthly expenses and reduce future repair costs.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Belimo can offer subscription services for performance monitoring and maintenance alerts, and sell durable, high‑efficiency actuators at competitive prices, capturing value through recurring revenue and volume sales.
assumptions: Homeowners prioritize long‑term cost savings over immediate premium features.
Belimo can provide clear evidence of energy savings and reduced maintenance costs.
Subscription services for performance monitoring are acceptable to consumers.
predictions: A survey of homeowners would show at least 40% indicating intent to purchase a Belimo smart thermostat if it promises annual energy savings of at least €200.
Sales of Belimo residential smart actuators would be higher in regions with higher average energy bills.
Customers would be more likely to recommend Belimo if they cite cost savings as a primary reason.

X1.name: Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Residential Smart HVAC Actuators
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging and a choice-based conjoint to measure premium willingness to pay and cost-saving willingness to pay.
X1.sample: 500 U.S. homeowners who have a central air conditioning system and have a programmable thermostat, recruited via an online panel.
X1.measure: 1) Premium willingness to pay: maximum price a respondent would pay for a Belimo smart thermostat compared to a competitor's smart thermostat. 2) Cost‑saving willingness to pay: maximum annual energy‑cost savings a respondent would accept as a trade‑off for a Belimo smart thermostat versus a competitor's smart thermostat.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Respondents will indicate a premium willingness to pay at least 20% above the competitor's price and a cost‑saving acceptance of at least $200 annual savings.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Respondents will indicate a premium willingness to pay at least 15% above the competitor's price and a cost‑saving acceptance of at least $200 annual savings.

X1.decision_rule: If the premium willingness to pay for Belimo exceeds the competitor's price by at least 20% AND the cost‑saving acceptance of $200 annual savings is met, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If either condition is not met, do not invest in a consumer expansion.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer reducing packing errors and does not address consumer willingness to pay for Belimo's residential smart actuators or any demand mechanism. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Public evidence shows Belimo already offers residential HVAC actuators and provides OEM support for residential HVAC projects, but no source shows consumer willingness to pay a premium for Belimo's specific smart actuators or actual purchase intent. The proposed willingness-to-pay survey is the next step.
final.target_customer: Homeowners with central air conditioning systems who have a programmable thermostat and are interested in energy efficiency and comfort.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated residential smart HVAC product that integrates Belimo's high‑efficiency actuators and valves with smart home capabilities, offering precise temperature control and potential energy savings.
final.next_action: Run the proposed willingness-to-pay survey (500 U.S. homeowners, 8 weeks, €15,000) to measure premium willingness to pay and cost‑saving acceptance.
final.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market, the willingness to pay a premium, and the competitive landscape for smart home thermostats remain uncertain.
would_change_if: If the survey shows a premium willingness to pay of at least 20% above a competitor's price and a cost‑saving acceptance of $200 annual savings, we would proceed to develop a consumer proposition.
If the survey shows no significant premium willingness to pay or low cost‑saving acceptance, we would maintain the current B2B focus and not pursue consumer expansion.

X1.name: Premium vs Cost-Saving Messaging Test for Residential Smart Actuators
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from regions with varying energy cost awareness. Participants see one of two product descriptions for a Belimo residential smart actuator: (A) Premium messaging emphasizing energy savings, precise temperature control, and smart home integration; (B) Cost-saving messaging emphasizing annual energy bill savings, reduced maintenance needs, and long-term investment. Participants then indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and maximum price they would pay.
X1.sample: 500 homeowners in three regions: high energy cost awareness (e.g., California), moderate (e.g., Texas), and low (e.g., Florida). Recruit via an online panel to ensure demographic diversity.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and maximum price willingness to pay for each messaging condition.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and higher maximum price for premium messaging in high‑energy‑cost regions.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and higher maximum price for cost‑saving messaging in high‑energy‑cost regions.

X1.decision_rule: If the difference in average purchase intent between premium and cost‑saving messaging is ≥ 1.5 points in high‑energy‑cost regions, proceed to develop a premium consumer proposition. If the difference is ≤ 1.5 points, focus on cost‑saving messaging. If both regions show similar differences, the premium proposition is not justified.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer reducing packing errors and does not address consumer demand for Belimo residential smart actuators, purchase intent, or willingness to pay. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., premium, energy‑saving smart HVAC actuators) targeting homeowners in high‑energy‑cost regions. Begin with a limited pilot to test purchase intent and willingness to pay before scaling.
final.target_customer: Homeowners in high‑energy‑cost regions (e.g., California, Texas) who are aware of energy costs and seek comfort and savings.
final.value_proposition: Belimo's integrated smart actuators offer precise temperature control, energy savings, and seamless smart home integration, allowing homeowners to reduce monthly bills and maintenance costs while maintaining comfort.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Premium vs Cost‑Saving Messaging Test (500 homeowners in three regions) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay. Use the decision rule: if the premium messaging difference is ≥1.5 points in high‑energy‑cost areas,
final.uncertainty: Consumer willingness to pay a premium for Belimo's specific smart actuators and the competitive landscape remain uncertain. The test will clarify these points before committing resources.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent for premium messaging below 30% in any region, the premium proposition would be reconsidered.
If a competitor offers a comparable smart actuator at a lower price, the investment case would weaken.

X1.method: Online survey with simulated home CPR kit offering. Participants are randomly assigned to one of three conditions: (A) Health responsibility condition (emphasizing personal family health protection). (B) Insurance/cost condition (emphasizing insurance coverage and low price). (C) Control condition (no framing). Participants indicate purchase intent at a price point of $50 and likelihood to purchase within 6 months.
X1.sample: 300 adult respondents recruited via an online panel, balanced across the three conditions.
X1.measure: Purchase intent rate (percentage of participants indicating "very likely" to purchase) and stated price sensitivity.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent in the health responsibility condition compared to the control and insurance conditions.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent in the insurance/cost condition compared to the control and health responsibility conditions.

X1.decision_rule: If the health responsibility condition exceeds the insurance/cost condition by at least 10 percentage points, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing personal health responsibility. If the insurance/cost condition exceeds the health responsibility condition by at least 10 percentage points, pursue an insurance-reimbursement or low-cost model. If neither condition exceeds the other by 10 points, do not expand into a consumer proposition.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes personal health responsibility and family protection, leveraging Laerdal’s existing home CPR program. Conduct a targeted test to validate purchase intent under health‑responsibility framing before scaling.
final.target_customer: Households with children or older adults who cite family health protection as a reason for seeking emergency preparedness.

X1.name: Home CPR Device Purchase Intent Pilot
X1.method: Online survey with randomized exposure to a home CPR training kit description and a time-saving CPR kit description. Participants are randomly assigned to view either the home CPR kit description or the time-saving CPR kit description. After viewing, participants are asked about purchase intent (1-7 scale) and willingness to pay (EUR).
X1.sample: 500 adults aged 18-65, recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and geographic region to reflect the U.S. population.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1-7) and willingness to pay (EUR) for each exposure.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay for the home CPR kit description compared to the time-saving CPR kit description.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay for the time-saving CPR kit description compared to the home CPR kit description.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent for the home CPR kit description is at least 1.5 points higher than for the time-saving CPR kit description (i.e., average home CPR intent = 5.5 vs. time-saving intent = 4), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for home CPR training. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, do not invest in a consumer proposition and continue focusing on B2B markets.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for home CPR training that emphasizes privacy, flexibility, and life-saving necessity. Begin with a limited pilot to test purchase intent and willingness to pay before scaling.
final.target_customer: Individual consumers aged 18-65 who are concerned about cardiac health and want to prepare for emergencies in the privacy of their home.
final.value_proposition: A portable, user-friendly home CPR training kit that allows learning at your own pace, in the comfort of your home, with clear instructions and a focus on life-saving skills.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Home CPR Device Purchase Intent Pilot (500 adults, 10 weeks, €15,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for the home CPR kit versus a time-saving CPR kit.
final.uncertainty: The actual purchase intent and willingness to pay from consumers are unknown; the pilot will determine whether the consumer demand justifies investment.
would_change_if: If the pilot shows purchase intent below 5% or willingness to pay significantly below €50, we would reconsider the consumer proposition and focus on B2B markets.
If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for time-saving CPR training, we would shift the focus to a time-saving consumer proposition.

X1.name: Branded vs Unbranded Home CPR Kit Purchase Test
X1.method: Randomized controlled online survey with a choice between a branded home CPR kit (Laerdal brand, regulatory certification) and an identical unbranded home CPR kit. Participants are recruited from households in the United States with at least one adult member. Each participant sees one of the two kits and is asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely) and to state the maximum price they would pay.
X1.sample: Proposed sample: 500 households (1,000 participants) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region to reflect the U.S. population.
X1.measure: Primary measure: average purchase intent score for the branded kit versus the unbranded kit. Secondary measure: maximum price participants would pay for the branded kit.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Branded kit will achieve a higher average purchase intent score than the unbranded kit, and the difference will be statistically significant (p < 0.05).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Unbranded kit will achieve a higher average purchase intent score than the branded kit, and the difference will be statistically significant (p < 0.05).

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent score for the branded kit is at least 1.5 points higher than the unbranded kit and the difference is statistically significant, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home CPR training). If the difference is less than 1.5 points or not statistically significant, do not invest in a consumer proposition at this time.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Public evidence shows Laerdal already offers a branded home CPR program (CPR Anytime) and that consumers are prepared to perform CPR in homes, but it does not demonstrate that consumers will purchase a branded home kit at a premium price. A controlled test is needed to measure purchase intent and price sensitivity.
final.target_customer: Individuals and families who need to be prepared for cardiac emergencies, particularly those who currently lack access to professional training.
final.value_proposition: A branded, regulated home CPR kit that delivers private, convenient training and can be shared with family members, leveraging Laerdal’s reputation and regulatory endorsement to justify a premium price.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Branded vs Unbranded Home CPR Kit Purchase Test (500 households, 10 weeks, €18,000) to measure purchase intent and price sensitivity before committing to a consumer product.
final.uncertainty: Whether consumers will actually purchase the branded kit at a premium price, and whether the perceived value of brand and regulation outweighs price sensitivity.
would_change_if: If the test shows the branded kit achieving a purchase intent difference of at least 1.5 points and a statistically significant p-value, we would proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition.
If the test shows the unbranded kit achieving higher purchase intent or that price sensitivity is high, we would reconsider the investment.

X1.name: Purchase Intent Test: Personal Health Responsibility vs Trust Messaging
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Participants view a product description of a home CPR training kit and are asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely). Randomly assigned to either a personal health responsibility message (emphasizing family protection and personal responsibility) or a trust message (emphasizing Laerdal's medical reputation and professional-grade safety).
X1.sample: 500 U.S. adults recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region to ensure representativeness.
X1.measure: Average purchase intent score for each condition.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Personal health responsibility message will yield a higher average purchase intent score than trust message.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Trust message will yield a higher average purchase intent score than personal health responsibility message.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent score for the personal health responsibility condition exceeds the trust condition by at least 1.5 points (e.g., 5.5 vs 4.0), proceed to develop a consumer proposition based on personal health responsibility. If the trust condition exceeds the personal condition by at least 1.5 points, develop a consumer proposition based on trust. If the difference is below 1.5 points, conclude insufficient evidence to justify investment and recommend no expansion.

revisions.reason: The simulated warehouse test (SYN-D) measures packing errors for a label printer and does not address consumer purchase intent, personal health responsibility, or trust messaging. Therefore it provides no evidence for or against T1.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for home CPR training, but first run the proposed purchase intent test to validate whether personal health responsibility messaging drives higher purchase intent than trust messaging. If the test confirms a 1.5-point advantage for the personal health responsibility condition, proceed to develop a consumer proposition; otherwise, reconsider the investment.
final.target_customer: Individual consumers (households) who are concerned about out-of-hospital cardiac arrests and want to be prepared to perform CPR in emergencies.
final.value_proposition: A portable, user-friendly home CPR training kit that empowers families to learn lifesaving skills in the comfort of their own home, leveraging Laerdal's medical reputation and personal health responsibility messaging.
final.next_action: Execute the purchase intent test (500 U.S. adults, randomized messaging conditions, 7-point scale, 1.5-point threshold) within the 8-week, €18,000 budget.
final.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market and the willingness to pay for a home CPR kit are uncertain. Regulatory approval for consumer use of CPR devices is also uncertain.
would_change_if: If the test shows the trust condition exceeds the personal health responsibility condition by at least 1.5 points, we would shift focus to a trust-based consumer proposition.
If the test shows no significant difference or the personal health responsibility condition wins, we would recommend no expansion and continue focusing on B2B markets.

arguments.name: Messaging Test: Insurance vs Lifestyle Messaging
arguments.method: Run a targeted online survey with two message variants for a home CPR device. Participants are recruited from two distinct geographic segments: a segment with strong insurance or legal requirements for home CPR training (e.g., California, New York) and a segment without such requirements (e.g., Texas). Each participant sees one of the two message variants and is asked to indicate their purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely).
arguments.sample: 500 adults (250 from each segment) to ensure sufficient statistical power.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent score on a 7-point scale for each message variant.

prediction_by_theory.T1: In the segment with insurance/legal requirements, the purchase intent score for the insurance message will be significantly higher than for the lifestyle message.
prediction_by_theory.T2: In the segment without insurance/legal requirements, the purchase intent score for the lifestyle message will be significantly higher than for the insurance message.

arguments.decision_rule: If the purchase intent score for the insurance message in the segment with requirements is at least 1.5 points higher than the lifestyle message, proceed to develop a consumer proposition focused on insurance/legal requirements. If neither difference is statistically significant, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.

X1.name: DIY vs Professional Installation Choice Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase and willingness-to-pay questions. Participants are randomly assigned to either a DIY scenario (low-cost, easy installation) or a Professional scenario (guaranteed installation, premium price). Both scenarios present Kingspan's insulation product at a fixed price point (e.g., £150 for a 2m x 1m board). Participants indicate their preferred choice and maximum price they would pay.
X1.sample: 500 UK homeowners (250 per arm) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, income, and energy concern levels.
X1.measure: Primary measure: proportion of participants choosing the DIY scenario vs Professional scenario. Secondary measure: average maximum price participants would pay for each scenario.

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 55% will choose the DIY scenario and be willing to pay up to £150.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 55% will choose the Professional scenario and be willing to pay up to £150.

X1.decision_rule: If DIY share ≥ 55% AND Professional share ≤ 45%, conclude T1 is supported. If Professional share ≥ 55% AND DIY share ≤ 45%, conclude T2 is supported. If neither condition is met, conclude no clear preference.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for DIY home insulation, leveraging Kingspan’s existing direct-to-consumer channel and DIY resources. Begin with a limited pilot to test demand and willingness to pay before scaling.
final.target_customer: UK homeowners seeking to improve home energy efficiency and reduce heating bills, particularly those who view DIY as a viable option.
final.value_proposition: Kingspan’s premium, high‑performance insulation sold directly or through DIY retailers, offering clear installation guidance and a simple, low‑cost upgrade path.
final.next_action: Run the proposed DIY vs Professional Installation Choice Test (500 UK homeowners, 6‑week online survey) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay. Use results to decide whether to proceed with a full consumer launch.
final.uncertainty: Actual purchase behavior and price sensitivity are unknown; the test will resolve whether homeowners will adopt DIY insulation at scale. Regulatory barriers (e.g., scheme requirements) and competitive landscape also remain uncertain.
would_change_if: If the test shows DIY share below 55% or willingness to pay below £150, we would reconsider the DIY focus and explore professional channels.

X1.name: Digital Messaging Test: Energy Savings vs Compliance Messaging
X1.method: Run a controlled online survey with two parallel messaging paths. Randomly assign 1,000 UK homeowners to either the Energy Savings path (highlighting personal cost savings and comfort improvements) or the Compliance path (highlighting mandatory building code requirements and government rebates). Both paths include a purchase intent question and a willingness-to-pay estimate.
X1.sample: 1,000 UK homeowners who have shown interest in home improvement (from a panel of DIY homeowners and energy-conscious consumers)
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and maximum willingness-to-pay (EUR) for each path

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and higher willingness-to-pay on the Energy Savings path
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and higher willingness-to-pay on the Compliance path

X1.decision_rule: If the Compliance path achieves purchase intent ≥ 30% and willingness-to-pay ≥ €1,200, proceed to develop a compliance-focused consumer proposition. If the Energy Savings path achieves purchase intent ≥ 30% and willingness-to-pay ≥ €1,200, develop an energy-saving consumer proposition. If neither path meets the thresholds, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer reducing packing errors and does not address consumer motivation for home insulation. It bears on no theory and does not affect the assessment of T1.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes personal energy cost savings and comfort improvements, supported by clear installation guidance. Use the proposed Digital Messaging Test to validate demand before scaling.
final.target_customer: DIY homeowners in the UK who are interested in home improvement and looking to reduce long-term energy bills and improve home comfort.
final.value_proposition: Kingspan's premium-priced insulation products, marketed on energy cost savings and comfort benefits, delivered directly to consumers through its online channel, leveraging its existing manufacturing capacity and brand reputation for quality
final.next_action: Run the Digital Messaging Test (1,000 homeowners, two messaging paths, purchase intent and willingness-to-pay thresholds) to determine whether to proceed with an energy-saving consumer proposition or maintain focus on construction
final.uncertainty: The primary uncertainty is whether homeowners are motivated primarily by energy cost savings (T1) or by regulatory compliance and government incentives (T2). The test will resolve this.
would_change_if: If the Compliance path achieves purchase intent ≥30% and willingness-to-pay ≥€1,200, the recommendation would shift to a compliance-focused consumer proposition.
If neither path meets the thresholds, the recommendation would remain to maintain focus on construction professionals.

X1.name: Digital Messaging Test: DIY vs Professional Insulation Proposition
X1.method: Run a targeted online survey with two distinct messaging paths. Recruit 1,000 UK homeowners who have completed a home improvement project in the past 12 months. Randomly assign participants to one of two groups: Group A receives a DIY-focused message emphasizing cost savings, environmental impact, and ease of installation; Group B receives a professional guidance message emphasizing expert installation, code compliance, and peace of mind. Both groups are presented with a product description of Kingspan's roof insulation and a price point (e.g., £150 for a 4m² roll). Participants are asked to indicate their purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely) and to state the primary reason for their choice.
X1.sample: 1,000 UK homeowners who have completed a home improvement project in the past 12 months, recruited via an online panel.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1-7) and primary reason for choosing (open-ended).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and will cite cost savings and environmental impact as the primary reason.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent and will cite professional guidance and code compliance as the primary reason.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent score for Group A is at least 5.5 points higher than Group B (i.e., Group A average >= 5.5 - Group B average), we conclude that T1 is more supported and recommend developing a differentiated consumer proposition focused on DIY motivation. If Group B's average is at least 5.5 points higher, we conclude T2 is more supported and recommend a professional guidance proposition. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, we conclude neither theory is strongly supported and recommend further market research.

final.value_proposition: Kingspan's premium-priced roof insulation sold directly to consumers via an online hub, offering clear DIY guidance, cost savings, and environmental benefits.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Digital Messaging Test (or a smaller pilot) to measure purchase intent and primary motivation. Use the decision rule to decide whether to proceed with a full consumer launch.
final.uncertainty: The actual willingness to pay for insulation and the relative importance of cost savings versus professional guidance are uncertain. Regulatory changes and competition from existing DIY brands also introduce risk.
would_change_if: If the pilot shows purchase intent below 3.5 out of 7 or if the primary reason is not cost savings or environmental impact, we would reconsider the DIY focus and explore professional guidance instead.

frame.objective: Determine whether Ansell Limited should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current industrial and healthcare protective gloves and body protection, and identify what public evidence would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available

Must assess current consumer reach and demand for protective gloves
Must consider competitive landscape and potential regulatory barriers
Any recommendation must be based on evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and feasibility
alternatives: Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, gardening, cycling) with a new product or marketing approach

T1.claim: Outdoor recreation participants treat protective gloves as a fashion accessory and a status symbol, so they would purchase multiple pairs at premium prices, giving Ansell a direct-to-consumer channel the opportunity to capture margin.
T1.who_benefits: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts who value style and status
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If gloves are perceived as fashion items rather than purely functional, consumers will buy multiple pairs to express identity and appear professional, shifting from single-use to multiple purchases.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Ansell can charge premium prices for branded, design-led consumer gloves and retain margin through direct sales, bypassing retail intermediaries.
assumptions: Outdoor recreation participants currently purchase protective gloves primarily for functional protection rather than style.
A design-led, branded consumer proposition can be successfully marketed to this segment.
Regulatory requirements for consumer gloves do not prevent premium pricing.
predictions: In a test offering a branded, design-led outdoor glove at a premium price, purchase intent among outdoor recreation participants will be at least 20% higher than for a generic functional glove.
Surveyed participants will cite style and status as primary reasons for purchase, not protection.
T1.first_claim: Outdoor recreation participants treat protective gloves as a fashion accessory and a status symbol, so they would purchase multiple pairs at premium prices, giving Ansell a direct-to-consumer channel the opportunity to capture margin.

T2.claim: Consumers purchase protective gloves primarily for functional protection and compliance, so a differentiated consumer proposition will not generate demand; the market is served by established industrial and healthcare suppliers, and Ansell's consumer presence is limited to licensing.
T2.who_benefits: Industrial and healthcare end-users who need gloves for job safety and regulatory compliance
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers do not purchase gloves for fashion or status; they buy them to meet safety standards and legal requirements, so a new consumer proposition will not change purchasing behaviour.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Ansell can capture value through licensing its brand and technology to consumer gloves manufacturers, retaining margin while leveraging its existing manufacturing capabilities.
assumptions: Consumer gloves are primarily purchased for functional protection and compliance, not style.
Existing industrial and healthcare suppliers already meet consumer demand.

frame.objective: Determine whether Ansell Limited should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current industrial and healthcare protective gloves and body protection, and identify what public evidence would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment
Must assess current consumer reach and demand for protective gloves
Must consider competitive landscape and potential regulatory barriers
Any recommendation must be based on evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and feasibility
alternatives: Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, gardening, cycling) with a new product or marketing approach

Maintain focus on industrial and healthcare segments and not pursue consumer expansion
License the Ansell brand or technology to consumer product manufacturers rather than creating a direct consumer offering

T1.claim: Outdoor recreation and gardening consumers will adopt differentiated protective gloves if they perceive them as a lifestyle accessory that enhances comfort and performance, leading to repeat purchases and premium pricing.
T1.who_benefits: Outdoor recreation and gardening enthusiasts who currently use generic or cheap gloves and seek a premium, brand-safe product.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Shifting from utilitarian to lifestyle positioning creates a perceived value beyond protection, making consumers willing to pay more for design, comfort, and brand association.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Ansell can capture value through premium pricing, brand licensing, and direct-to-consumer e-commerce sales of differentiated designs, leveraging its existing design capabilities.
assumptions: Outdoor and gardening markets are large enough to support a differentiated consumer proposition
Consumers associate protective gloves with lifestyle brands and are willing to pay a premium
Ansell can adapt its design and manufacturing capabilities to meet consumer expectations without compromising industrial performance
predictions: A survey of outdoor recreation participants will show >50% would purchase a branded protective glove at a price 20% above generic gloves
Sales of a differentiated consumer line will generate higher average revenue per unit than existing industrial gloves
Brand awareness among target consumers will increase when marketed as lifestyle accessories
T1.first_claim: Outdoor recreation and gardening consumers will adopt differentiated protective gloves if they perceive them as a lifestyle accessory that enhances comfort and performance, leading to repeat purchases and premium pricing.

T2.claim: Healthcare and cleanroom professionals will adopt differentiated protective gloves if they perceive them as a safety-critical, high-performance product that meets stringent regulatory standards, leading to repeat purchases and willingness to pay premium prices.
T2.who_benefits: Healthcare providers, cleanroom facilities, and medical professionals who require gloves that meet or exceed regulatory requirements for sterility, durability, and performance.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Regulatory compliance and the need for reliable protection in high-risk environments create a demand for gloves that are not just functional but also certified and trusted, prompting professionals to choose brands with proven safety records
T2.how_value_is_captured: Ansell can capture value through premium pricing, certification compliance marketing, and partnerships with healthcare suppliers, leveraging its existing cleanroom and surgical product expertise.
assumptions: Healthcare and cleanroom markets are large and growing, with consistent demand for compliant protective gloves
Regulatory standards for gloves are clear and enforceable, creating a barrier to entry for lower-quality products
Ansell's existing cleanroom and surgical product capabilities can be adapted to meet consumer compliance requirements
predictions: A survey of healthcare professionals will show >60% would purchase a branded protective glove at a price 15% above generic gloves if it carries a certification stamp
Sales of a differentiated consumer line will generate higher average revenue per unit than existing industrial gloves in the healthcare segment
Brand awareness among target consumers will increase when marketed as safety-critical, compliant products

X1.name: Consumer Proposition Test: Lifestyle vs. Regulatory Positioning
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.
X1.sample: 500 respondents: 250 outdoor recreation/gardening enthusiasts and 250 healthcare/cleanroom professionals, recruited via panel providers.
X1.measure: Percentage of respondents who would purchase a differentiated glove at a specified price (e.g., 20% premium for lifestyle, 15% premium for regulatory compliance) and average WTP per respondent.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Outdoor recreation group will show >50% willingness to pay a 20% premium for lifestyle positioning.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Healthcare/cleanroom group will show >60% willingness to pay a 15% premium for regulatory compliance positioning.

X1.decision_rule: If the outdoor group meets or exceeds 50% WTP at the 20% premium threshold, proceed to develop a lifestyle consumer proposition. If the healthcare group meets or exceeds 60% WTP at the 15% premium threshold, proceed to develop a regulatory compliance consumer proposition. If neither threshold is met, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a warehouse label printer reducing packing errors and does not address consumer demand, pricing, or lifestyle positioning for protective gloves. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Public evidence shows Ansell's focus remains on industrial and healthcare segments, and no source demonstrates consumer demand for a lifestyle proposition. A proposed test (Consumer Proposition Test: Lifestyle vs. Regulatory Positioning) is needed to validate willingness to pay before committing resources.
final.target_customer: Outdoor recreation and gardening enthusiasts who currently use generic or cheap gloves and seek a premium, brand-safe product.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated protective glove line positioned as a lifestyle accessory that enhances comfort and performance, offering premium pricing and brand safety for outdoor activities.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Proposition Test: Lifestyle vs. Regulatory Positioning to measure willingness to pay and validate demand before any product development.
final.uncertainty: The size of the outdoor recreation market and consumer willingness to pay a premium for protective gloves are uncertain. Regulatory compliance demand for healthcare gloves is also uncertain.
would_change_if: If the test shows >50% of outdoor recreation respondents willing to pay a 20% premium for lifestyle positioning, we would reconsider developing a lifestyle consumer proposition.
If the test shows >60% of healthcare professionals willing to pay a 15% premium for regulatory compliance positioning, we would reconsider developing a regulatory compliance consumer proposition.

T1.who_benefits: Outdoor enthusiasts and fashion-conscious consumers who value style and brand identity.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Shifting perception from purely functional to fashion-driven, increasing willingness to buy multiple pairs and pay a premium.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Ansell can capture value through premium pricing, brand extension, and direct-to-consumer sales channels.
assumptions: Consumers currently view protective gloves as utilitarian rather than fashion items.

Ansell can effectively communicate a fashion-driven proposition without compromising functionality.
predictions: Surveyed outdoor recreation participants will indicate higher intent to purchase gloves for fashion reasons compared to functional reasons.

T2.why_behaviour_changes: Increased awareness of safety risks and regulatory requirements for outdoor activities creates a perceived need for protective gear, prompting purchase even at higher price points.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Ansell can capture value through premium pricing justified by safety credentials, partnerships with outdoor brands, and targeted marketing emphasizing risk mitigation.
assumptions: Outdoor recreation participants are aware of safety risks associated with their activities.
Regulatory or insurance requirements for outdoor activities increase demand for protective gloves.
Ansell can effectively communicate safety benefits without compromising performance.
predictions: Surveyed outdoor recreation participants will indicate higher purchase intent for gloves when framed as safety essential versus fashion.

X1.name: Fashion vs Safety Messaging Test for Outdoor Gloves
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition and purchase intent measurement.
X1.sample: 500 adult outdoor recreation participants recruited via outdoor forums and social media, balanced across two conditions (Fashion vs Safety messaging).
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and willingness to pay (EUR). Secondary: repeat purchase intent.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Fashion condition will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Safety condition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Safety condition will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Fashion condition.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent in the Fashion condition exceeds the Safety condition by at least 10 percentage points (e.g., 45% vs 35%), proceed to develop a fashion-focused consumer proposition. If the Safety condition exceeds by at least 10 points, develop a safety-focused proposition. If neither condition exceeds 10 points, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.

final.target_customer: Outdoor recreation participants who engage in activities with inherent risk (e.g., hiking, climbing, cycling) and value safety.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition that positions protective gloves as a fashion accessory and status symbol for outdoor enthusiasts, leveraging Ansell's brand and design capabilities to capture premium pricing and brand extension.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Fashion vs Safety messaging test (500 participants, EUR 18,000, 8 weeks) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay under fashion versus safety messaging.
final.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market for fashion-driven protective gloves and the willingness of consumers to pay a premium for such products are uncertain. The test will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows the Safety condition exceeds the Fashion condition by at least 10 percentage points, we would shift focus to a safety-focused consumer proposition.
If neither condition exceeds 10 points, we would maintain the current focus on industrial and healthcare segments.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Public evidence shows Ansell focuses on core industrial and healthcare segments and has exited retail household gloves. There is no demonstrated consumer demand, willingness to pay, or specific use case for outdoor recreation or gardening. The proposed test (X1) is needed to validate purchase intent and price premium before committing resources.

frame.objective: Determine whether Ansell Limited should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current industrial and healthcare protective gloves and body protection, and identify what public evidence would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment
Must assess current consumer reach and demand for protective gloves
Must consider competitive landscape and potential regulatory barriers
Any recommendation must be based on evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and feasibility
alternatives: Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, gardening, cycling) with a new product or marketing approach
Expand the existing consumer presence through existing channels (e.g., e‑commerce, retail partnerships) without a new differentiated proposition
Maintain focus on industrial and healthcare segments and not pursue consumer expansion
License the Ansell brand or technology to consumer product manufacturers rather than creating a direct consumer offering

T1.claim: Outdoor recreation and gardening consumers will purchase differentiated protective gloves if they perceive them as a fashion accessory that enhances their activity experience, leading to higher repeat purchases and premium pricing.
T1.who_benefits: Outdoor recreation and gardening enthusiasts who currently use generic or disposable gloves and seek a stylish, durable alternative that aligns with their lifestyle.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If gloves are repositioned as a fashion item, consumers will shift from buying generic gloves to investing in a dedicated protective line, increasing purchase frequency and willingness to pay a premium.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Ansell can capture value through premium pricing, brand differentiation, and direct-to-consumer or retail partnerships that leverage its design capabilities and consumer research expertise.
assumptions: Consumers associate protective gear with style and are willing to pay more for branded, differentiated products.
The outdoor recreation market is large enough to support a differentiated consumer proposition without cannibalizing industrial or healthcare sales.
Regulatory requirements for protective gear can be met without compromising design or brand image.
predictions: Surveyed outdoor recreation participants will indicate higher intent to purchase a branded protective glove compared to an unbranded one.
Sales of the differentiated consumer line will show higher repeat purchase rates than generic gloves.
Willingness-to-pay studies will show a premium price premium of at least 20% over standard protective gloves.
T1.first_claim: Outdoor recreation and gardening consumers will purchase differentiated protective gloves if they perceive them as a fashion accessory that enhances their activity experience, leading to higher repeat purchases and premium pricing.

T2.claim: Healthcare and cleanroom professionals will adopt differentiated protective gloves if they perceive them as a safety-critical, high-performance product that reduces incident rates and improves compliance, leading to increased purchase and repeat purchase.
T2.who_benefits: Healthcare providers, cleanroom facilities, and medical staff who currently use standard gloves and seek a product that demonstrably reduces errors and enhances safety.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: If gloves are positioned as a safety-critical, high-performance product with proven incident reduction, professionals will shift from generic gloves to a differentiated line, increasing purchase frequency and willingness to pay a premium.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Ansell can capture value through premium pricing, safety certification marketing, and partnerships with healthcare suppliers that emphasize performance and compliance benefits.
assumptions: Healthcare professionals prioritize safety and are willing to pay more for gloves that demonstrably reduce incident rates.
Regulatory requirements for cleanroom and medical gloves can be met without compromising performance.
The healthcare segment remains a profitable growth area for Ansell.
predictions: Healthcare professionals will report higher satisfaction with a differentiated glove compared to standard gloves.
Purchase intent for the differentiated line will be higher among healthcare staff than among non-healthcare consumers.
Willingness-to-pay studies will show a premium price premium of at least 15% over standard gloves.

X1.name: Differentiated Glove Proposition Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized exposure to a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation or healthcare). Participants view a product description, price, and purchase intent questions.
X1.sample: 300 respondents: 150 outdoor recreation enthusiasts and 150 healthcare professionals, recruited via panel providers to ensure geographic diversity.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and willingness-to-pay (WTP) premium (percentage above standard glove price). Secondary measure: repeat purchase intent over 12 months.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Outdoor recreation participants will show higher purchase intent and WTP premium than healthcare professionals.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Healthcare professionals will show higher purchase intent and WTP premium than outdoor recreation participants.

X1.decision_rule: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition if either group exceeds the respective threshold (e.g., outdoor recreation purchase intent >= 30% and WTP premium >= 20% of standard glove price, or healthcare purchase intent >= 30% and WTP premium >= 20%). If neither meets the threshold, do not pursue expansion.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a warehouse label printer reducing packing errors and does not address consumer demand, fashion perception, or purchase intent for differentiated protective gloves. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Public evidence shows Ansell focuses on core industrial and healthcare segments and has exited retail household gloves. There is no demonstrated consumer demand, willingness to pay, or specific use case for outdoor recreation or gardening. The proposed test (X1) is needed to validate purchase intent and price premium before committing resources.
final.target_customer: Outdoor recreation and gardening enthusiasts who currently use generic or disposable gloves and seek a stylish, durable alternative that aligns with their lifestyle.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated protective glove line positioned as a fashion accessory that enhances outdoor activities, offering premium design, durability, and brand differentiation.
final.next_action: Run the proposed differentiated Glove Proposition Test (X1) to measure purchase intent and willingness-to-pay premium among outdoor recreation participants.
final.uncertainty: The size of the outdoor recreation market, consumer willingness to pay a premium for fashion-protective gloves, and the ability to meet regulatory requirements without compromising design.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent below 30% or willingness-to-pay premium below 20% of standard glove price, the investment would be reconsidered.
If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for healthcare-protective gloves or a clear use case for cleanroom professionals, the recommendation would shift toward that segment.
